| <samp class="listingcharacter">document.lastModified</samp> | Contains the date when the document was last modified |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">document.URL</samp> | Contains a URL of the current document |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">document.domain</samp> | Contains the domain of the current document |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">document.cookie</samp> | Contains a list of all cookies for the document |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">document.forms</samp> | Contains a list of all forms in the document |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">document.images</samp> | Contains a list of all images in the document |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">document.links</samp> | Contains a list of all links in the document |

**Table 5.1**     Selected Properties of the document Object

###### DOM under Node.js

The DOM in the form of the global <samp class="listingcharacter">document</samp> variable is only available in browser-based runtime environments. Node.js, for example (see [Chapter 17](#17_001.html_h17)), doesn’t provide any such global variable because Node.js isn’t typically used to render web pages. Under Node.js, a DOM of a web page can only be created via special modules such as jsdom ([https://github.com/jsdom/jsdom](https://github.com/jsdom/jsdom)), which can be used to parse web pages.

The structure of the DOM—which properties and methods are available, which node types are provided, and so on—is defined in the DOM application programming interface (API), a specification of the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). This API is independent of the programming language; that is, there are implementations not only for JavaScript, but also for other programming languages like Java or C++.

###### Interface, Implementation, and API

In object-oriented programming, interfaces are used to define the methods that must be present in implementations (i.e., concrete realizations of the respective interface). An API defines a set of interfaces provided by a software system.

Accordingly, the DOM API is a set of interfaces that browsers provide for working with web pages.

## 5.2    Selecting Elements

Whether you want to change existing information on a web page or add new information, you must first select an element on the web page that you want to change or to which you want to attach the new information. For this purpose, the DOM API offers various properties and methods, as shown in [Table 5.2](#05_002.html_t5.2).

As you can see, there are some methods that return multiple elements and other methods that return single elements. We'll look at the details in the following sections.

| Property/Method | Description | Return Code | Section |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementById()</samp> | Selects an element based on an ID | Single element | [Section 5.2.1](#05_002.html_h5.2.1) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsBy-ClassName()</samp> | Selects elements based on a class name | List of elements | [Section 5.2.2](#05_002.html_h5.2.2) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsBy-TagName()</samp> | Selects all elements with the specified element name | List of elements | [Section 5.2.3](#05_002.html_h5.2.3) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsBy-Name()</samp> | Selects elements by their name | List of elements | [Section 5.2.4](#05_002.html_h5.2.4) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">querySelector()</samp> | Returns the first element that matches a given CSS selector | Single element | [Section 5.2.5](#05_002.html_h5.2.5) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">querySelectorAll()</samp> | Returns all elements that match a given CSS selector | List of elements | [Section 5.2.5](#05_002.html_h5.2.5) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">parentElement</samp> | Returns the parent element for a node | Single element | [Section 5.2.6](#05_002.html_h5.2.6) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">parentNode</samp> | Returns the parent node for a node | Single node | [Section 5.2.6](#05_002.html_h5.2.6) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">previousElement-Sibling</samp> | Returns the previous sibling element for a node | Single element | [Section 5.2.8](#05_002.html_h5.2.8) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">previousSibling</samp> | Returns the previous sibling node for a node | Single node | [Section 5.2.8](#05_002.html_h5.2.8) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">nextElementSibling</samp> | Returns the next sibling element for a node | Single element | [Section 5.2.8](#05_002.html_h5.2.8) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">nextSibling</samp> | Returns the next sibling node for a node | Single node | [Section 5.2.8](#05_002.html_h5.2.8) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">firstElementChild</samp> | Returns the first child element for a node | Single element | [Section 5.2.7](#05_002.html_h5.2.7) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">firstChild</samp> | Returns the first child node for a node | Single node | [Section 5.2.7](#05_002.html_h5.2.7) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">lastElementChild</samp> | Returns the last child element for a node | Single element | [Section 5.2.7](#05_002.html_h5.2.7) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">lastChild</samp> | Returns the last child node for a node | Single node | [Section 5.2.7](#05_002.html_h5.2.7) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">childNodes</samp> | Returns all child nodes for a node | List of nodes | [Section 5.2.7](#05_002.html_h5.2.7) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">children</samp> | Returns all child elements for a node | List of elements | [Section 5.2.7](#05_002.html_h5.2.7) |

**Table 5.2**     The Different Methods and Properties for Selecting Elements

###### Selection Methods

Selection methods and properties are not only available for the document node, but also for other nodes ([Section 5.2.9](#05_002.html_h5.2.9)).

### 5.2.1    Selecting Elements by ID

Elements on a web page can be assigned an ID (which is unique on that web page) via the <samp class="listingcharacter">id</samp> attribute. This ID can be used in CSS rules, and you can select the corresponding element via JavaScript using the <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementById()</samp> method of the <samp class="listingcharacter">document</samp> object. You simply pass the ID of the element to be selected to the method in the form of a string.

In [Listing 5.2](#05_002.html_l5.2), the element with the <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> ID is selected (see also [Figure 5.4](#05_002.html_f5.4)) and stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter">mainElement</samp> variable. Then, the <samp class="listingcharacter">className</samp> property is used to change the <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> attribute of the element to the value <samp class="listingcharacter">border</samp>, which in the example results in the element having a red border with rounded corners (see [Figure 5.5](#05_002.html_f5.5); the complete example, including HTML and CSS code, can be found in the download area for the book).

```
const mainElement = document.getElementById('main');
mainElement.className = 'border'; 
```

**Listing 5.2**     Accessing an Element via the ID

[![The getElementById() Method Selects One Element at Most](bilderklein/klein05_004.png)](img-f5.4.html)

**Figure 5.4** The getElementById() Method Selects One Element at Most

[![The Returned Element Is Assigned a New CSS Class, Giving the Element a Highlighted Border](bilderklein/klein05_005.png)](img-f5.5.html)

**Figure 5.5**     The Returned Element Is Assigned a New CSS Class, Giving the Element a Highlighted Border

###### Tip

In practice, it's not a bad idea to program a little more defensively and check that a variable to be accessed is not <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">undefined</samp>. This also applies to working with the DOM, as the <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementById()</samp> method returns the value <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> if no element with the passed ID is found. If you then try to access a property or method on the assumed element, a runtime error occurs. To prevent this, you should use an <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> query to ensure that the return value of <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementById()</samp> is not <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>, as shown in [Listing 5.3](#05_002.html_l5.3).

```
const mainElement = document.getElementById('main'); // Select element by ID.
if(mainElement !== null) {                           // If the element 
                                                     // is not empty,
  mainElement.className = 'border';                  // assign new CSS class.
}
```

**Listing 5.3**     If There Is No Element with the main ID, the Variable Is Not Accessed

Alternatively, you can shorten the code and take advantage of the <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> operator, where the second operand is only evaluated if the first operand returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>. Thus, in [Listing 5.4](#05_002.html_l5.4), the operand <samp class="listingcharacter">(mainElement.className = 'border')</samp> is evaluated (or executed) only if <samp class="listingcharacter">mainElement</samp> has a value that does not evaluate to <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>—in other words, is not <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>.

```
const mainElement = document.getElementById('main'); // Select element by ID.
mainElement && (mainElement.className = 'border');
```

**Listing 5.4**     You Can Use the && Operator to Shorten This Check

The check is even shorter using the optional chaining operator <samp class="listingcharacter">?</samp>, which has only been available since ES2020\. In [Listing 5.5](#05_002.html_l5.5), the <samp class="listingcharacter">className</samp> property is accessed only when <samp class="listingcharacter">mainElement</samp> is not <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">undefined</samp>.

```
const mainElement = document.getElementById('main'); // Select element by ID.
mainElement?.className = 'border';
```

**Listing 5.5**You Can Use the ? Operator to Check whether a Property Is Defined

###### Performance of Selection Methods

Compared to other selection methods, selecting an element by ID is quite fast in terms of performanceas a web page isn’t allowed to have multiple elements with the same ID, and thus the search can very quickly find the appropriate element for an ID. Other selection methods, like the <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByClassName()</samp> method presented in the next section, are much slower in comparison because they require checking every element on the web page. You usually won't notice the speed difference, but you should keep it in mind.

###### Tip

You shouldn’t overuse DOM methods. If you need to use the result of a DOM method in multiple places within a program, store the result in a variable instead of calling the DOM method over and over again. Consider that every call of a DOM method that searches for elements in the DOM tree will cost computing time. This computing time can be minimized by using variables for caching results.

### 5.2.2    Selecting Elements by Class

Like IDs, CSS classes can be assigned to individual elements on a web page. These classes are managed via the <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> attribute. An element can have multiple classes, and unlike IDs, multiple elements can have the same class.

This, in turn, results in the corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByClassName()</samp> DOM method—which enables the selection by CSS class—returning not only a single element, but several elements, if necessary.

As an argument, the method is passed the class name as a string, as shown in [Listing 5.6](#05_002.html_l5.6). In this example, all elements containing the <samp class="listingcharacter">even</samp> CSS class are selected—that is, the two even table rows (see [Figure 5.6](#05_002.html_f5.6)).

```
const tableRowsEven = document
    .getElementsByClassName('even');      // Select all even table rows. 
```

**Listing 5.6**     Accessing an Element by Class Name

[![The getElementsByClassName() Method Can Return Multiple Elements](bilderklein/klein05_006.png)](img-f5.6.html)

**Figure 5.6**     The getElementsByClassName() Method Can Return Multiple Elements

The return value of <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByClassName()</samp> is a node list (more precisely, an object of the <samp class="listingcharacter">NodeList</samp> type), which is used in a similar way as an array (but which is not an array; more about that in a moment). This node list contains the elements in the exact order in which they appear on the web page.

Although node lists look like arrays at first glance, they are not arrays. This is a fact that JavaScript beginners must always keep in mind as its nonobservance frequently leads to errors in the program.

A feature that node lists have in common with arrays is that you can access the individual elements in a node list via an index. That is, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">tableRowsEven[0]</samp>, for example, to access the first element, <samp class="listingcharacter">tableRowsEven[1]</samp> to access the second element, and so on. Another common feature is the <samp class="listingcharacter">length</samp> property, which can be used to determine the number of elements in the node list.

So, for example, to iterate over all elements of a node list, you can proceed as shown in [Listing 5.7](#05_002.html_l5.7). This listing uses a <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop to iterate over all elements of the list. As with iteration over real arrays, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">length</samp> property and the access by index. Using these features, the example assigns a new background color to each element in the list (see [Figure 5.7](#05_002.html_f5.7)).

```
const tableRowsEven = document
  .getElementsByClassName('even');              // Select all even 
                                                // table rows.
if(tableRowsEven.length > 0) {                  // If at least one element 
                                                // is found.
  for(let i=0; i<tableRowsEven.length; i++) {   // Iterate all elements.
    const tableRow = tableRowsEven[i];          // Assign element to a variable.
    tableRow.style.backgroundColor = '#CCCCCC'; // Set new background color.
  }
} 
```

**Listing 5.7**     Iteration over a List of Nodes Using the Array Syntax

[![The Even Table Cells Were Assigned a Different Background Color via JavaScript](bilderklein/klein05_007.png)](img-f5.7.html)

**Figure 5.7**     The Even Table Cells Were Assigned a Different Background Color via JavaScript

###### Modifying the CSS of an Element

The <samp class="listingcharacter">style</samp> property of an element allows you to access or modify the CSS properties of an element. The object stored in this property contains all CSS properties as object properties (<samp class="listingcharacter">style.color</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">style.border</samp>, etc.). For CSS properties such as <samp class="listingcharacter">background-color</samp> that contain a hyphen, the corresponding object properties are defined in CamelCase notation (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">style.backgroundColor</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">style.fontFamily</samp>).

As an alternative to the array syntax with square brackets, individual nodes of a node list can be accessed using the <samp class="listingcharacter">item()</samp> method. In this case, the argument to be passed is the index of the element to be returned. The loop above could also be rephrased as shown in [Listing 5.8](#05_002.html_l5.8).

```
const tableRowsEven = document
  .getElementsByClassName('even');              // Select all even 
                                                // table rows.
if(tableRowsEven.length > 0) {                  // If at least one element 
                                                // is found.
  for(let i=0; i<tableRowsEven.length; i++) {   // Iterate all elements.
    const tableRow = tableRowsEven.item(i);     // Assign element to a variable.
    tableRow.style.backgroundColor = '#CCCCCC'; // Set new background color.
  }
} 
```

**Listing 5.8**     Iteration over a List of Nodes Using the item() Method

###### Method Borrowing

Because node lists aren’t real arrays (they are objects of the <samp class="listingcharacter">NodeList</samp> type) but array-like objects (like the <samp class="listingcharacter">arguments</samp> object, remember?), in practice you’ll often use the technique of method borrowing (see [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4)) to still be able to use <samp class="listingcharacter">Array</samp> methods (see [Listing 5.9](#05_002.html_l5.9)).

```
Array.prototype.forEach.call(tableRowsEven, (tableRow) => {
  tableRow.style.backgroundColor = '#CCCCCC';
}); 
```

**Listing 5.9**     Iteration over a Node List via Method Borrowing

###### Active Node Lists versus Static Node Lists

A distinction is made between active and static node lists. The former are node lists in which changes made to individual nodes in the list have a direct impact on the web page; that is, the changes are immediately reflected on the web page.

With the latter, on the other hand, changes to nodes within the node list have no direct effect on the web page; they are not immediately reflected. The <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByClassName()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByTagName()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByName()</samp> methods return active node lists, whereas the <samp class="listingcharacter">querySelectorAll()</samp> method returns a static node list.

### 5.2.3    Selecting Elements by Element Name

The <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByTagName()</samp> method can be used to select elements by their element name. The method expects the name of the element. For example, to select all table cells (see [Figure 5.8](#05_002.html_f5.8)), proceed as shown in [Listing 5.10](#05_002.html_l5.10).

[![The getElementsByTagName() Method Selects Elements by Their Element Name](bilderklein/klein05_008.png)](img-f5.8.html)

**Figure 5.8**     The getElementsByTagName() Method Selects Elements by Their Element Name

First, all table cells are selected via the <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByTagName()</samp> method, and then each element is assigned a new font and a new font size. The results are displayed in [Figure 5.9](#05_002.html_f5.9).

```
const tableCells = document.getElementsByTagName('td');
if(tableCells.length > 0) {                  // If at lease one element is 
                                             // found.
  for(let i=0; i<tableCells.length; i++) {   // Iterate all elements.
    const tableCell = tableCells[i];         // Assign element to a variable.
    tableCell.style.fontFamily = 'Verdana';  // Set new font.
    tableCell.style.fontSize = '9pt';        // Set new font size.
  }
} 
```

**Listing 5.10**     Accessing an Element via Element Name

[![The Table Cells Are Assigned a New Font and Font Size](bilderklein/klein05_009.png)](img-f5.9.html)

**Figure 5.9**     The Table Cells Are Assigned a New Font and Font Size

###### Note

Ensure that you only pass the name of the element to the <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByTagName()</samp> method, without additional angle brackets or the like. For example, the <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByTagName('<td>')</samp> call wouldn’t work.

### 5.2.4    Selecting Elements by Name

Some elements can be assigned a <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> attribute in HTML—for example <samp class="listingcharacter"><input></samp> elements of the <samp class="listingcharacter">radio</samp> type—to indicate their association with a selection group. In [Listing 5.11](#05_002.html_l5.11), for example, the three radio buttons are assigned to the <samp class="listingcharacter">genre</samp> group.

```
<form action="">
  <label for="artist">Artist</label>
  <input id="artist" type="text" name="artist">
  <br>
  <label for="album">Album</label>
  <input id="album" type="text" name="album">
  <br>
  <p>Genre:</p>
  <fieldset>
    <input type="radio" id="st" name="genre" value="Stonerrock">
    <label for="st">Stonerrock</label>
    <br>
    <input type="radio" id="sp" name="genre" value="Spacerock">
    <label for="sp">Spacerock</label>
    <br>
    <input type="radio" id="ha" name="genre" value="Hardrock">
    <label for="ha">Hardrock</label>
  </fieldset>
</form> 
```

**Listing 5.11**     A Simple HTML Form

Using the <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByName()</samp> method, elements can be selected based on this <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> attribute. In [Listing 5.12](#05_002.html_l5.12), this method is used to select all elements with a <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> attribute of the value <samp class="listingcharacter">genre</samp>. (The other two form elements with the values <samp class="listingcharacter">artist</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">album</samp> are not selected, though; see [Figure 5.10](#05_002.html_f5.10).)

[![The getElementsByName() Method Selects Elements by Their name Attribute](bilderklein/klein05_010.png)](img-f5.10.html)

**Figure 5.10**     The getElementsByName() Method Selects Elements by Their name Attribute

In loop in [Listing 5.12](#05_002.html_l5.12), the values of these elements (<samp class="listingcharacter">inputElement.value</samp>) are output: <samp class="listingcharacter">Stonerrock</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Spacerock</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Hardrock</samp>.

```
const inputElementsForGenre = document
  .getElementsByName('genre');                          // Select all elements 
                                                        // by name.
if(inputElementsForGenre.length > 0) {                  // If at least one 
                                                        // element is found.
  for(let i=0; i<inputElementsForGenre.length; i++) {   // Iterate all elements.
    const inputElement = inputElementsForGenre[i];      // Assign element to a 
                                                        // variable.
    console.log(inputElement.value);                    // Output: Stonerrock, 
                                                        // Spacerock, Hardrock
  }
} 
```

**Listing 5.12**     Accessing Elements by Element Names

###### Browser Support of getElementsByName()

The <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByName()</samp> method doesn’t work consistently in all browsers. For example, in some versions of the Internet Explorer and Opera browsers, the method returns not only those elements with a <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> attribute that matches the passed value, but also those with an <samp class="listingcharacter">id</samp> attribute that matches the passed value. In my opinion, the other selection methods (presented so far and to be presented in a moment) provide sufficient possibilities for selecting elements so that you can actually do without this method in practice.

### 5.2.5    Selecting Elements by Selector

The DOM methods for selecting elements presented so far already accomplish a lot but are quite restricted in the form of expression. The element you want to select might not have an ID or class at all; the <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementById()</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByClassName()</samp> methods don’t help in such cases. The <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByTagName()</samp> method, on the other hand, is very unspecific because it tends to select many elements. And <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByName()</samp> should be used with caution anyway, for the reasons mentioned earlier.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">querySelector()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">querySelectorAll()</samp> methods are much more versatile and expressive for returning elements for a given CSS selector. The former method returns the first element that matches the corresponding CSS selector, while the latter method returns all elements that match the CSS selector.

[Listing 5.13](#05_002.html_l5.13) shows an example of using <samp class="listingcharacter">querySelector()</samp>. This example passes the <samp class="listingcharacter">#main table td:nth-child(2)</samp> CSS selector, which describes the second table cells of each row (<samp class="listingcharacter">td:nth-child(2)</samp>) inside a table (<samp class="listingcharacter">table</samp>) within an element with the <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> ID (<samp class="listingcharacter">#main</samp>). But because the <samp class="listingcharacter">querySelector()</samp> method selects only the first element matching a selector, only the first <samp class="listingcharacter"><td></samp> element is returned (see [Figure 5.11](#05_002.html_f5.11) and [Figure 5.12](#05_002.html_f5.12)).

```
const tableCell = document.querySelector('#main table td:nth-child(2)');
tableCell.style.border = 'thick solid red'; 
```

**Listing 5.13**     Accessing an Element by CSS Selector

[![The querySelector() Method Returns at Most One Element](bilderklein/klein05_011.png)](img-f5.11.html)

**Figure 5.11** The querySelector() Method Returns at Most One Element

[![The querySelector() Method Returns the First Element That Matches the CSS Selector](bilderklein/klein05_012.png)](img-f5.12.html)

**Figure 5.12**     The querySelector() Method Returns the First Element That Matches the CSS Selector

[Listing 5.14](#05_002.html_l5.14), on the other hand, shows the use of the <samp class="listingcharacter">querySelectorAll()</samp> method. This listing uses the same CSS selector as above. This time, however, you receive all elements that match this selector—that is, all second <samp class="listingcharacter"><td></samp> elements (see [Figure 5.13](#05_002.html_f5.13)).

```
const tableCells = document.querySelectorAll('#main table td:nth-child(2)');
if(tableCells.length > 0) {
  for(let i=0; i<tableCells.length; i++) {
    const tableCell = tableCells[i];
    tableCell.style.border = 'thick solid red';
  }
} 
```

**Listing 5.14**     Accessing Multiple Elements by CSS Selector

[![The querySelectorAll() Method Can Return Multiple Elements](bilderklein/klein05_013.png)](img-f5.13.html)

**Figure 5.13**     The querySelectorAll() Method Can Return Multiple Elements

Within the loop, these elements are then marked with a red frame in the same way as before (see [Figure 5.14](#05_002.html_f5.14)).

[![The querySelectorAll() Method Returns All Elements That Match the Passed CSS Selector](bilderklein/klein05_014.png)](img-f5.14.html)

**Figure 5.14**     The querySelectorAll() Method Returns All Elements That Match the Passed CSS Selector

Web developers have long waited for the capabilities offered by <samp class="listingcharacter">querySelector()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">querySelectorAll()</samp>. Before the introduction of the Selector API (for the current version, see [www.w3.org/TR/selectors4](http://www.w3.org/TR/selectors4)), which defines these two important methods and others, you had to make do with the DOM methods for selecting elements presented previously.

The jQuery library recognized this limitation and provided corresponding helper functions quite early. In [Chapter 10](#10_001.html_h10), we’ll discuss this aspect of this well-known JavaScript library, among other topics.

Overall, the methods for selecting elements via CSS selectors make the work of a JavaScript developer much easier. An overview of the different CSS selectors is shown in [Table 5.3](#05_002.html_t5.3).

| Selector | Description | Since CSS version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> | Selects every element | 2 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">E</samp> | Selects elements of type <samp class="listingcharacter">E</samp> | 1 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[a]</samp> | Selects elements with the attribute <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> | 2 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[a="b"]</samp> | Selects elements with the attribute <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> that has the value <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> | 2 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[a~="b"]</samp> | Selects elements with the attribute <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> the value of which is a list of values, one of which is equal to <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> | 2 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[a^="b"]</samp> | Selects elements with the attribute <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> the value of which starts with <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[a$="b"]</samp> | Selects elements with the attribute <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> the value of which ends with <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[a*="b"]</samp> | Selects elements with the attribute <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> the value of which contains <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> as a substring | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">[a&#124;="b"]</samp> | Selects elements with the attribute <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> the values of which are a series of values separated by minus signs, where the first value is <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> | 2 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:root</samp> | Selects the root element of a document | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:nth-child(n)</samp> | Selects the nth child element of an element | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:nth-last-child(n)</samp> | Selects the nth child element of an element starting from the end | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:nth-of-type(n)</samp> | Selects the nth sibling element of a specific type of an element | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:nth-last-of-type(n)</samp> | Selects the nth sibling element of a specific type of an element starting from the end | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:first-child</samp> | Selects the first child element of an element | 2 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:last-child</samp> | Selects the last child element of an element | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:first-of-type</samp> | Selects the first sibling element of an element | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:last-of-type</samp> | Selects the last sibling element of an element | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:only-child</samp> | Selects elements that are the only child element of their parent element | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:only-of-type</samp> | Selects elements that are the only element of their type among their sibling elements | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:empty</samp> | Selects elements that have no child elements | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:link</samp> | Selects links that have not yet been clicked | 2 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:visited</samp> | Selects links that have already been clicked | 2 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:active</samp> | Selects links that are being clicked at that moment | 2 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:hover</samp> | Selects links over which the mouse is currently located | 2 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:focus</samp> | Selects links that are currently focused | 2 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:target</samp> | Selects jump labels that can be reached via links within a web page | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:lang(en)</samp> | Selects elements the <samp class="listingcharacter">lang</samp> attribute of which has the value <samp class="listingcharacter">en</samp> | 2 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:enabled</samp> | Selects form elements into which values can be entered or which can be operated (and are not disabled) | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:disabled</samp> | Selects form elements that cannot be operated or for which input has been disabled via the <samp class="listingcharacter">disabled</samp> attribute | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:checked</samp> | Selects checkboxes and radio buttons that are enabled | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">.className</samp> | Selects elements the <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> attribute of which has the value <samp class="listingcharacter">className</samp> | 1 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">#main</samp> | Selects elements the <samp class="listingcharacter">id</samp> attribute of which has the value <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> | 1 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">:not(s)</samp> | Selects elements that do not match the selector <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> specified in parentheses | 3 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">E F</samp> | Selects elements of type <samp class="listingcharacter">F</samp> that occur somewhere within an element of type <samp class="listingcharacter">E</samp> | 1 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">E > F</samp> | Selects elements of type <samp class="listingcharacter">F</samp> that are child elements of an element of type <samp class="listingcharacter">E</samp> | 2 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">E + F</samp> | Selects elements of type <samp class="listingcharacter">F</samp> that are sibling elements immediately following an element of type <samp class="listingcharacter">E</samp> | 2 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">E ~ F</samp> | Selects elements of type <samp class="listingcharacter">F</samp> that are sibling elements of an element of type <samp class="listingcharacter">E</samp> | 3 |

**Table 5.3**     The Different Selectors in CSS3

### 5.2.6    Selecting the Parent Element of an Element

Element nodes have various properties that allow you to access related elements. Related elements are parent nodes or elements, child nodes or elements, and sibling nodes or elements.

For the selection of parent nodes/elements, the <samp class="listingcharacter">parentNode</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">parentElement</samp> properties are available; for the selection of child nodes/elements, there are the <samp class="listingcharacter">firstChild</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">firstElementChild</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">lastChild</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">lastElementChild</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">childNodes</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">children</samp> properties; and for the selection of sibling nodes/elements, the <samp class="listingcharacter">previousSibling</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">previousElementSibling</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">nextSibling</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">nextElementSibling</samp> properties are provided.

These characteristics will be explained in a little more detail ahead. Let's start with the selection of parent nodes or elements.

To select the parent node of an element (or node), the <samp class="listingcharacter">parentNode</samp> property is available, while the parent element can be selected via the <samp class="listingcharacter">parentElement</samp>. In most cases, the parent node is always an element as well; that is, the <samp class="listingcharacter">parentNode</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">parentElement</samp> properties contain the same value (see [Listing 5.15](#05_002.html_l5.15) and [Figure 5.15](#05_002.html_f5.15)).

```
const table = document.querySelector('table');
console.log(table.parentNode);    // <main>
console.log(table.parentElement); // <main> 
```

**Listing 5.15**     Accessing a Parent Node or Parent Element

[![Selection of the Parent Element](bilderklein/klein05_015.png)](img-f5.15.html)

**Figure 5.15**     Selection of the Parent Element

###### Nodes and Elements

Not all nodes in the DOM tree are elements, but all elements are always nodes.

It’s important to understand that some of the preceding properties return nodes, while other properties return elements. The <samp class="listingcharacter">parentNode</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">childNodes</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">firstChild</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">lastChild</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">previousSibling</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">nextSibling</samp> properties return nodes, while the <samp class="listingcharacter">parentElement</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">children</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">firstElementChild</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">lastElementChild</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">previousElementSibling</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">nextElementSibling</samp> properties return elements.

The following example illustrates what this means in practice. Look at the HTML code in [Listing 5.16](#05_002.html_l5.16) and its DOM in [Figure 5.16](#05_002.html_f5.16). They show a relatively simple web page with only two <samp class="listingcharacter"><span></samp> elements inside the <samp class="listingcharacter"><body></samp> element, each enclosed in text.

```
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
  Text
  <span></span>
  Text
  <span></span>
  Text
</body>
</html> 
```

**Listing 5.16**     A Simple HTML Example

[![Overview of the Different Forms of Access](bilderklein/klein05_016.png)](img-f5.16.html)

**Figure 5.16**     Overview of the Different Forms of Access

Accordingly, the corresponding DOM below the <samp class="listingcharacter"><body></samp> element contains (in this order) a text node, an element node, a text node, an element node, and again a text node. For all these nodes, the <samp class="listingcharacter"><body></samp> element represents both the parent node and the parent element at the same time. Thus, for all these nodes, the <samp class="listingcharacter">parentNode</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">parentElement</samp> properties return the same value: the <samp class="listingcharacter"><body></samp> element.

Also, you can see in the DOM in [Figure 5.16](#05_002.html_f5.16) that the <samp class="listingcharacter">parentNode</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">parentElement</samp> properties generally always reference the same element for all nodes. The only exception is the <samp class="listingcharacter"><html></samp> element. This element does not have a parent element but "only" a parent node—the document node. In this case, the <samp class="listingcharacter">parentElement</samp> property returns the value <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>.

The other relationships between elements and nodes in the DOM will be discussed in the following sections.

### 5.2.7    Selecting the Child Elements of an Element

The child elements of an element can be determined via the <samp class="listingcharacter">children</samp> property, the child nodes via the <samp class="listingcharacter">childNodes</samp> property. Whether an element has child nodes can be determined using the <samp class="listingcharacter">hasChildNodes()</samp> method, which returns a Boolean value. You can determine whether an element has child elements using the <samp class="listingcharacter">childElementCount</samp> property: this contains the number of child elements.

[Listing 5.17](#05_002.html_l5.17) shows some examples (again related to the HTML from [Listing 5.1](#05_001.html_l5.1)). You see that the <samp class="listingcharacter"><tbody></samp> element has four child elements (the four <samp class="listingcharacter"><tr></samp> elements; see [Figure 5.17](#05_002.html_f5.17)) and a total of nine child nodes (see [Figure 5.18](#05_002.html_f5.18)).

[![Selection of All Child Elements](bilderklein/klein05_017.png)](img-f5.17.html)

**Figure 5.17**     Selection of All Child Elements

```
const tbody = document.querySelector('tbody');
console.log(tbody.children.length);    // 4
console.log(tbody.childElementCount);  // 4
console.log(tbody.childNodes.length);  // 9
console.log(tbody.hasChildNodes());    // true 
```

**Listing 5.17**     Accessing Child Nodes or Child Elements

[![Selection of All Child Nodes](bilderklein/klein05_018.png)](img-f5.18.html)

**Figure 5.18**     Selection of All Child Nodes

The reason for this is that although no text occurs between, before, and behind the four <samp class="listingcharacter"><tr></samp> elements in HTML, so-called whitespace nodes are produced (see the following box). These whitespace nodes are created whenever line breaks are used between two elements in HTML, for example.

###### Whitespace Nodes

Whitespace within the HTML code, created by spaces, tabs, or line breaks, for example, always results in text nodes without text being created in the DOM. These are referred to as whitespace nodes.

In addition, various other properties are available that can be used to select individual child elements or child nodes:

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">firstChild</samp> property contains the first child node.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">lastChild</samp> property contains the last child node.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">firstElementChild</samp> property contains the first child element.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">lastElementChild</samp> property contains the last child element.

[Listing 5.18](#05_002.html_l5.18) shows some examples. The result of selecting the first and last child elements is shown in [Figure 5.19](#05_002.html_f5.19), and the result of selecting the first and last child nodes is illustrated in [Figure 5.20](#05_002.html_f5.20).

```
const tbody = document.querySelector('tbody');
console.log(tbody.firstChild);           // Text node
console.log(tbody.lastChild);            // Text node
console.log(tbody.firstElementChild);    // <tr>
console.log(tbody.lastElementChild);     // <tr> 
```

**Listing 5.18**     Accessing Specific Child Nodes and Child Elements

###### Note

In most cases, you’ll probably work with element nodes. In these cases, it’s best to use properties that also return element nodes (such as <samp class="listingcharacter">firstElementChild</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">lastElementChild</samp>). There was a time when web developers only had properties available that returned all types of nodes (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">firstChild</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">lastChild</samp>) and they had to filter element nodes based on the node type itself. Fortunately, this has changed.

[![Selection of the First and the Last Child Element](bilderklein/klein05_019.png)](img-f5.19.html)

**Figure 5.19** Selection of the First and the Last Child Element

[![Selection of the First and the Last Child Node](bilderklein/klein05_020.png)](img-f5.20.html)

**Figure 5.20** Selection of the First and the Last Child Node

### 5.2.8    Selecting the Sibling Elements of an Element

Now you know how to select nodes/elements in the DOM tree above (parent nodes/parent elements) and below (child nodes/child elements) a starting node/element using its properties. In addition, there is also the possibility to select the sibling nodes or sibling elements within one level of the DOM:

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">previousSibling</samp> property contains the previous sibling node.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">nextSibling</samp> property contains the next sibling node.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">previousElementSibling</samp> property contains the previous sibling element.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">nextElementSibling</samp> property contains the next sibling element.

A code example is shown in [Listing 5.19](#05_002.html_l5.19). Starting from the second table row, first the previous sibling node (via <samp class="listingcharacter">previousSibling</samp>) and the next sibling node (via <samp class="listingcharacter">nextSibling</samp>) are selected, both being text nodes—or more precisely, whitespace nodes (see [Figure 5.21](#05_002.html_f5.21)).

```
const tableCell = document.querySelector('tbody tr:nth-child(2)');
console.log(tableCell.previousSibling);        // Text node
console.log(tableCell.nextSibling);            // Text node
console.log(tableCell.previousElementSibling); // <tr>
console.log(tableCell.nextElementSibling);     // <tr> 
```

**Listing 5.19**     Accessing Specific Sibling Nodes and Sibling Elements

[![Selection of the Previous and the Next Sibling Node](bilderklein/klein05_021.png)](img-f5.21.html)

**Figure 5.21**     Selection of the Previous and the Next Sibling Node

Then <samp class="listingcharacter">previousElementSibling</samp> selects the previous sibling element, and <samp class="listingcharacter">nextElementSibling</samp> selects the next sibling element (see [Figure 5.22](#05_002.html_f5.22)).

[![Selection of the Previous and the Next Sibling Element](bilderklein/klein05_022.png)](img-f5.22.html)

**Figure 5.22**     Selection of the Previous and the Next Sibling Element

### 5.2.9    Calling Selection Methods on Elements

Most of the presented DOM methods for selecting elements (<samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByClassName()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByTagName()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">querySelector()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">querySelectorAll()</samp>) can be called not only on the document node (i.e., on <samp class="listingcharacter">document</samp>), but also on all other element nodes of a web page (just <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementById()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByName()</samp> can be called only on the document node). In this case, the search for the elements includes only the subtree below the element on which the respective method was called.

Consider the HTML code in [Listing 5.20](#05_002.html_l5.20), which contains nested lists. In the JavaScript code shown in [Listing 5.21](#05_002.html_l5.21), the <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementsByTagName()</samp> method with the argument <samp class="listingcharacter">li</samp> is first called on the <samp class="listingcharacter">document</samp> node (which selects all list entries of the entire web page; see [Figure 5.23](#05_002.html_f5.23)) and then on the nested list with the <samp class="listingcharacter">list-2</samp> ID (which, in turn, selects only those list entries that occur in this subtree of the DOM—i.e., below the nested list; see [Figure 5.24](#05_002.html_f5.24)).

```
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head lang="en">
    <title>Example of the selection of elements</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <main id="main-content">
      <ul id="list-1">
        <li>List entry 1</li>
        <li>
          List entry 2
          <ul id="list-2">
            <li>List entry 2.1</li>
            <li>List entry 2.2</li>
            <li>List entry 2.3</li>
            <li>List entry 2.4</li>
          </ul>
        </li>
        <li>List entry 3</li>
        <li>List entry 4</li>
      </ul>
    </main>
  </body>
</html> 
```

**Listing 5.20**     Example HTML Page

```
const allListItemElements = document.getElementsByTagName('li');
console.log(allListItemElements.length); // Output: 8
const subList = document.getElementById('list-2');
const subListListItems = subList.getElementsByTagName('li');
console.log(subListListItems.length);    // Output: 4 
```

**Listing 5.21**     Selection of Elements Starting from a Parent Element

[![Calling the getElementsByTagName() Method on the Document Node](bilderklein/klein05_023.png)](img-f5.23.html)

**Figure 5.23** Calling the getElementsByTagName() Method on the Document Node

[![Calling the getElementsByTagName() Method on the <ul> Element with the list-2 ID](bilderklein/klein05_024.png)](img-f5.24.html)

**Figure 5.24**     Calling the getElementsByTagName() Method on the <ul> Element with the list-2 ID

### 5.2.10    Selecting Elements by Type

In addition to the presented selection methods, the <samp class="listingcharacter">document</samp> object provides various properties for accessing specific elements of a web page directly, see [Table 5.4](#05_002.html_t5.4). For example, the <samp class="listingcharacter">anchors</samp> property can be used to select all anchors (i.e., jump elements) on a web page, <samp class="listingcharacter">forms</samp> to select all forms, <samp class="listingcharacter">images</samp> to select all images, and <samp class="listingcharacter">links</samp> to select all links. In addition, the <samp class="listingcharacter">head</samp> property is available to access the <samp class="listingcharacter"><head></samp> element directly, and the <samp class="listingcharacter">body</samp> property can be used for direct access to the <samp class="listingcharacter"><body></samp> element.

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">document.anchors</samp> | Contains a list of all anchors of the web page |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">document.forms</samp> | Contains a list of all forms on the web page |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">document.images</samp> | Contains a list of all images on the web page |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">document.links</samp> | Contains a list of all links on the web page |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">document.head</samp> | Provides access to the <samp class="listingcharacter"><head></samp> element of the web page |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">document.body</samp> | Provides access to the <samp class="listingcharacter"><body></samp> element of the web page |

**Table 5.4**     Various Properties for Selecting Elements by Type

## 5.3    Working with Text Nodes

Once you’ve selected one or more elements, you can modify them: you can add or remove text, add or remove attributes, and add or remove elements. [Table 5.5](#05_003.html_t5.5) shows an overview of the main properties and methods available for this purpose, which we’ll discuss in detail in the following sections.

As mentioned before, any text on a web page is represented as text nodes within the DOM tree. Now let's take a look at how you can access and also modify the text contents.

| Property/Method | Description | Section |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">textContent</samp> | This property allows you to access the text content of a node. | [Section 5.3.1](#05_003.html_h5.3.1) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">nodeValue</samp> | This property allows you to access the contents of a node. | [Section 5.3.1](#05_003.html_h5.3.1) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">innerHTML</samp> | This property allows you to access the HTML content of a node. | [Section 5.3.3](#05_003.html_h5.3.3) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">createTextNode()</samp> | This method allows you to create text nodes. | [Section 5.3.4](#05_003.html_h5.3.4) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">createElement()</samp> | This method allows you to create elements. | [Section 5.4.1](#05_004.html_h5.4.1) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">createAttribute()</samp> | This method allows you to create attribute nodes. | [Section 5.5.3](#05_005.html_h5.5.3) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">appendChild()</samp> | This method allows you to add nodes to the DOM tree. | [Section 5.4.1](#05_004.html_h5.4.1) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">removeChild()</samp> | This method allows you to remove nodes from the DOM tree. | [Section 5.4.2](#05_004.html_h5.4.2) |

**Table 5.5**     The Different Methods and Properties for Modifying Elements

### 5.3.1    Accessing the Text Content of an Element

To access the plain text content of an element, it’s best to use the <samp class="listingcharacter">textContent</samp> property. This property is convenient because any HTML markup within the respective element is ignored and excluded from the returned value. The next two listings illustrate this. First, [Listing 5.22](#05_003.html_l5.22) shows a simple HTML list with one entry, where the contained text is marked up using <samp class="listingcharacter"><strong></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter"><em></samp> elements.

```
<ul id="news">
  <li>
    <strong>Record news: </strong>New album by <em>Ben Harper</em> released.
  </li>
</ul> 
```

**Listing 5.22**     HTML with Nested Elements

If you now access the <samp class="listingcharacter">textContent</samp> property as shown in [Listing 5.23](#05_003.html_l5.23), you’ll see that it contains only the plain text of the <samp class="listingcharacter"><li></samp> element, but not the <samp class="listingcharacter"><strong></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter"><em></samp> markup it contains.

```
const textContent = document.querySelector('#news li:nth-child(1)').textContent;
console.log(textContent);
// Output: Record news: New album by Ben Harper released. 
```

**Listing 5.23**     The textContent Property Ignores Markup within the Corresponding Element

###### Note

The <samp class="listingcharacter">textContent</samp> property is very convenient because in practice, when accessing the text content of an element, it’s often not relevant whether/what additional markup has been used.

### 5.3.2    Modifying the Text Content of an Element

If you want to reset the text content of an element, you also use the <samp class="listingcharacter">textContent</samp> property. As a value, you simply pass the new text, as shown in [Listing 5.24](#05_003.html_l5.24). Here, a new text is assigned to the list element used previously.

```
const element = document.querySelector('#news li:nth-child(1)');
element.textContent = 'Record news: New album by Tool not yet 
  released.'; 
```

**Listing 5.24**     The textContent Property Can Be Used to Reset the Text Content of an Element

Note, however, that <samp class="listingcharacter">textContent</samp> doesn’t enable you to add HTML markup: although the string passed in the following listing contains markup, it is not interpreted but displayed as text (see [Figure 5.25](#05_003.html_f5.25)).

```
const element = document.querySelector('#news li:nth-child(1)');
element.textContent = '<strong>Record news:</strong> New album by 
  <em>Tool</em> not yet released.'; 
```

**Listing 5.25**     The Markup within the Specified String Is Not Evaluated

[![Markup Specified via textContent Is Not Evaluated](bilderklein/klein05_025.png)](img-f5.25.html)

**Figure 5.25**     Markup Specified via textContent Is Not Evaluated

###### textContent versus innerText

In some browsers, you can also use the <samp class="listingcharacter">innerText</samp> property, which works in a similar way to <samp class="listingcharacter">textContent</samp> but is slightly different in detail. It is also not included in the DOM API and is thus not supported by Firefox, for example. We therefore advise that you avoid <samp class="listingcharacter">innerText</samp> and use <samp class="listingcharacter">textContent</samp> instead, as shown in the examples.

### 5.3.3    Modifying the HTML below an Element

If you want to insert not only text but also HTML into an element, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">innerHTML</samp> property. You’ll learn about another possibility later, DOM manipulation, which in practice is often used to add HTML to the DOM. For starters, however, or for adding simple HTML components, <samp class="listingcharacter">innerHTML</samp> is sufficient. An example is shown in [Listing 5.26](#05_003.html_l5.26): the same HTML block is added as in [Listing 5.25](#05_003.html_l5.25), but this time it is also interpreted as HTML (see [Figure 5.26](#05_003.html_f5.26)).

```
const element = document.querySelector('#news li:nth-child(1)');
element.innerHTML = '<strong>Record news:</strong> New album by <em>Tool 
  </em> not yet released.' 
```

**Listing 5.26**     The innerHTML Property Is Used to Evaluate Markup Contained in the Passed String

[![As Expected, the HTML Inserted via innerHTML Is Evaluated](bilderklein/klein05_026.png)](img-f5.26.html)

**Figure 5.26** As Expected, the HTML Inserted via innerHTML Is Evaluated

Conversely, you can also use <samp class="listingcharacter">innerHTML</samp> to read the HTML content of an element. As with <samp class="listingcharacter">textContent</samp>, the result is a string that now contains not only the text content but also the HTML markup (see [Listing 5.27](#05_003.html_l5.27)).

```
const innerHTML = document.querySelector('#news li:nth-child(1)').innerHTML;
console.log(innerHTML);
// Output: <strong>Record news: </strong>New album by 
// <em>Ben Harper</em> released. 
```

**Listing 5.27**     The innerHTML Property Also Contains the HTML Markup

### 5.3.4    Creating and Adding Text Nodes

As an alternative to the options shown for accessing or modifying the text within a web page via the <samp class="listingcharacter">textContent</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">innerHTML</samp> properties, there is still the possibility to create text nodes and add them manually to the DOM tree. For this purpose, the DOM API provides the <samp class="listingcharacter">createTextNode()</samp> method. In [Listing 5.28](#05_003.html_l5.28), a text node (with the text <samp class="listingcharacter">Example</samp>) is created via this method and then added to an existing element as a child node using the <samp class="listingcharacter">appendChild()</samp> method (more on this later). (This second step is necessary because the text node is not yet added to the DOM tree via the <samp class="listingcharacter">createTextNode()</samp> method.)

```
const element = document.getElementById('container');
const textNode = document.createTextNode('Example');
element.appendChild(textNode); 
```

**Listing 5.28**     Creating and Adding a Text Node

###### Other Methods for Creating Nodes

In addition to the <samp class="listingcharacter">createTextNode()</samp> method, there are other methods for creating nodes, including <samp class="listingcharacter">createElement()</samp> for creating element nodes ([Section 5.4.1](#05_004.html_h5.4.1)) and <samp class="listingcharacter">createAttribute()</samp> for creating attribute nodes ([Section 5.5.3](#05_005.html_h5.5.3)).

###### Document Node Methods

The <samp class="listingcharacter">createTextNode()</samp> method and also the <samp class="listingcharacter">createElement()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">createAttribute()</samp> methods described ahead are only available on the document node (i.e., the <samp class="listingcharacter">document</samp> object). These methods cannot be called on other nodes (and thus not on elements).

## 5.4    Working with Elements

Elements, too, can be created manually via methods and then added to the DOM tree (as opposed to using the <samp class="listingcharacter">innerHTML</samp> property, where you pass the HTML elements indirectly in the form of the text you assign to the property).

In this section, we’ll show you how to create and add elements using these methods and how to work with elements in general.

### 5.4.1    Creating and Adding Elements

To create elements, use the <samp class="listingcharacter">createElement()</samp> method. This method expects the name of the element to be created as a parameter and returns the new element. By calling the method, the new element is not yet added to the DOM, though (same as with text nodes when using the <samp class="listingcharacter">createTextNode()</samp> method).

However, several other methods are available for adding generated elements to the DOM:

*   Using <samp class="listingcharacter">insertBefore()</samp>, the element can be added as a child element before another element/node—that is, defined as a previous sibling element.

*   Using <samp class="listingcharacter">appendChild()</samp>, the element can be added as the last child element of a parent element.

*   Using <samp class="listingcharacter">replaceChild()</samp>, an existing child element (or an existing child node) can be replaced with a new child element. The method is called on the parent element and expects the new child node as the first parameter and the child node to be replaced as the second parameter.

###### Adding Text Nodes

By the way, these methods are also available for adding text nodes ([Section 5.3.4](#05_003.html_h5.3.4)).

A somewhat more complex—but practical—example is shown in [Listing 5.29](#05_004.html_l5.29). Here an HTML table is generated based on a contact list (which is represented in the form of an array). The individual entries in the contact list contain the first name, the last name, and the email address of each contact.

```
const contacts = [
  {
    firstName: 'John',
    lastName: 'Doe',
    email: 'john.doe@javascripthandbuch.de'
  },
  {
    firstName: 'James',
    lastName: 'Doe',
    email: 'james.doe@javascripthandbuch.de'
  },
  {
    firstName: 'Peter',
    lastName: 'Doe',
    email: 'peter.doe@javascripthandbuch.de'
  }
];

function createTable() {
  const tableBody = document.querySelector('#contact-table tbody');
  for(let i=0; i<contacts.length; i++) {
    // For the current contact ...
    const contact = contacts[i];
    // ... a new line is created.
    // (1)
    const tableRow = document.createElement('tr');
    // Within the row, different cells are created ... 
    // (2)
    const tableCellFirstName = document.createElement('td');
    // ... and filled with values.
    // (3)
    const firstName = document.createTextNode(contact.firstName);
    // (4)
    tableCellFirstName.appendChild(firstName);
    // (5)
    const tableCellLastName = document.createElement('td');
    // (6)
    const lastName = document.createTextNode(contact.lastName);
    // (7)
    tableCellLastName.appendChild(lastName);
    // (8)
    const tableCellEmail = document.createElement('td');
    // (9)
    const email = document.createTextNode(contact.email);
    // (10)
    tableCellEmail.appendChild(email);
    // (11)
    tableRow.appendChild(tableCellFirstName);
    // (12)
    tableRow.appendChild(tableCellLastName);
    // (13)
    tableRow.appendChild(tableCellEmail);
    // (14)
    tableBody.appendChild(tableRow);
  }
} 
```

**Listing 5.29**     Creating a Table Based on the Contact List

Everything related to the creation of the corresponding elements takes place within the <samp class="listingcharacter">createTable()</samp> function. Here, the <samp class="listingcharacter">querySelector()</samp> method first selects the <samp class="listingcharacter"><tbody></samp> element of the table that already exists in the HTML (see [Listing 5.30](#05_004.html_l5.30)) and then iterates the array containing the contact information. For each entry, the <samp class="listingcharacter">createElement()</samp> method is used to create a table row (<samp class="listingcharacter"><tr></samp>) and to create a table cell (<samp class="listingcharacter"><td></samp>) for each of the previously mentioned properties (<samp class="listingcharacter">firstName</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">lastName</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">email</samp>). Using the <samp class="listingcharacter">createTextNode()</samp> method, text nodes are created for the values of the properties and added to the respective <samp class="listingcharacter"><td></samp> element via <samp class="listingcharacter">appendChild()</samp> (alternatively, you could also use the <samp class="listingcharacter">textContent</samp> property here).

At the end of each iteration, the created table cells are then added as child elements to the corresponding table row, and in the last row of the iteration, the table row is added as a child element of the table body—that is, the <samp class="listingcharacter"><tbody></samp> element. The individual steps are explained using comments in the listing and can be traced with the help of [Figure 5.27](#05_004.html_f5.27).

```
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head lang="en">
  <title>Contacts Example</title>
</head>
<body onload="createTable()">
<main id="main-content">
  <h1>Contacts</h1>
  <table id="contact-table" summary="Contacts">
    <thead>
    <tr>
      <th>First name</th>
      <th>Last name</th>
      <th>E-mail address</th>
    </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
    </tbody>
  </table>
</main>
<script src="scripts/main.js"></script>
</body>
</html> 
```

**Listing 5.30**     The HTML Template

[![Sequence of Steps](bilderklein/klein05_027.png)](img-f5.27.html)

**Figure 5.27**     Sequence of Steps

### 5.4.2    Removing Elements and Nodes

To remove elements (or more generally nodes) from a parent element (or more generally a parent node), the <samp class="listingcharacter">removeChild()</samp> method is available. This method expects the element (or node) to be removed and also returns it as a return value. In [Listing 5.31](#05_004.html_l5.31) (based on the listings from the previous section), you can see a method for filtering table data (<samp class="listingcharacter">sortByFirstName()</samp>) that takes advantage of the <samp class="listingcharacter">removeChild()</samp> method to remove all child nodes and child elements from the table body (i.e., all table rows).

```
function sortByFirstName() {
  const tableBody = document.querySelector('#contact-table tbody');
  while (tableBody.firstChild !== null) {
    tableBody.removeChild(tableBody.firstChild);
  }
  contacts.sort(function(contact1, contact2) {
    return contact1.firstName.localeCompare(contact2.firstName);
  })
  createTable();
} 
```

**Listing 5.31**     Example of Using the removeChild() Method

### 5.4.3    The Different Types of HTML Elements

Every HTML element is represented by a specific object type within a DOM tree. These are set out in an extension to the DOM API called the DOM HTML specification. For example, links (<samp class="listingcharacter"><a></samp> elements) are represented by the <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLAnchorElement</samp> type, tables (<samp class="listingcharacter"><table></samp> elements) by the <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLTableElement</samp> type, and so on. An overview of the different HTML elements and their corresponding object types is given in [Table 5.6](#05_004.html_t5.6). Obsolete types are italicized within the table.

###### The HTMLElement Supertype

All object types have the same supertype—that is, the <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLElement</samp> type. Elements that have no specific type are assigned the <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLElement</samp> type by default.

###### Obsolete Elements

For the sake of completeness, the elements and object types that have become obsolete in the meantime are still listed in the table in italics.

| <samp class="listingcharacter"><strong></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><style></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLStyleElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><sub></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><sup></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><table></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLTableElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><tbody></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLTableSectionElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><td></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLTableCellElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><textarea></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLTextAreaElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><tfoot></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLTableSectionElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><th></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLTableHeaderCellElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><thead></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLTableSectionElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><time></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLTimeElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><title></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLTitleElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><tr></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLTableRowElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><tt></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><u></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><track></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLTrackElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><ul></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLUListElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><var></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLElement</samp> |
|  | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLUnknownElement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><video></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLVideoElement</samp> |

**Table 5.6**     The Different HTML Elements and Their Respective Types in JavaScript

[Listing 5.32](#05_004.html_l5.32) shows the principle of these object types using the example of tables represented by the <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLTableElement</samp> type. This type—like all the other types shown in [Table 5.6](#05_004.html_t5.6)—has individual properties corresponding to the type, including the <samp class="listingcharacter">caption</samp> property, which contains the subtitle of a table (and is <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> in the example, because the table in [Listing 5.1](#05_001.html_l5.1) has no <samp class="listingcharacter">caption</samp> attribute); the <samp class="listingcharacter">tHead</samp> property, which contains the header area—that is, the <samp class="listingcharacter"><thead></samp> element—of a table; the <samp class="listingcharacter">tBodies</samp> property, which contains the various table bodies—that is, <samp class="listingcharacter"><tbody></samp> elements—of a table; the <samp class="listingcharacter">rows</samp> property, which contains the table rows (including those in the header area); and the <samp class="listingcharacter">tFoot</samp> property, which contains the footer area—that is, the <samp class="listingcharacter"><tfoot></samp> element.

```
const table = document.querySelector('table');
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(table));  // HTMLTableElement
console.log(table.caption);                 // null
console.log(table.tHead);                   // thead
console.log(table.tBodies);                 // [tbody]
console.log(table.rows);                    // [tr, tr, tr, tr, tr]
console.log(table.tFoot);                   // null 
```

**Listing 5.32**     Each HTML Element Is Represented by Its Own Object Type

Besides individual properties, the different object types also have different methods: for example, the <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLTableElement</samp> type, shown in [Listing 5.33](#05_004.html_l5.33), contains the <samp class="listingcharacter">insertRow()</samp> method (among others), which can be used to directly create a new table row (without manually creating corresponding HTML elements via <samp class="listingcharacter">document.createElement()</samp>). This method returns an object of the type <samp class="listingcharacter">HTMLTableRowElement</samp>, which, in turn, comprises the <samp class="listingcharacter">insertCell()</samp> method (among others), via which a new table cell can be added directly to the corresponding row. In the example, a new table row with three cells is created in this way. This is much clearer than the example in [Listing 5.29](#05_004.html_l5.29), don't you think?

```
const newRow   = table.insertRow(1);
const newCellFirstName  = newRow.insertCell(0);
newCellFirstName.textContent = 'Bob';
const newCellLastName  = newRow.insertCell(1);
newCellLastName.textContent = 'Doe';
const newCellEmail  = newRow.insertCell(2);
newCellEmail.textContent = 'bob.doe@javascripthandbuch.de'; 
```

**Listing 5.33**     The Different Object Types Also Have Individual Methods

###### Property Names versus Element Names

Note that object properties like <samp class="listingcharacter">tHead</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">tBodies</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">tFoot</samp> are written in CamelCase notation, while the corresponding HTML elements are written in lowercase (<samp class="listingcharacter"><thead></samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><tbody></samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><tfoot></samp>).

## 5.5    Working with Attributes

The DOM API provides several methods for working with attributes:

*   You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">getAttribute()</samp> method to access the attributes of an element ([Section 5.5.1](#05_005.html_h5.5.1)).

*   You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">setAttribute()</samp> method to change the value of an attribute or to add attributes to an element ([Section 5.5.2](#05_005.html_h5.5.2)).

*   You can create attribute nodes via the <samp class="listingcharacter">createAttribute()</samp> method and add them using <samp class="listingcharacter">setAttributeNode()</samp> ([Section 5.5.3](#05_005.html_h5.5.3)).

*   You can remove attributes using the <samp class="listingcharacter">removeAttribute()</samp> method ([Section 5.5.4](#05_005.html_h5.5.4)).

### 5.5.1    Reading the Value of an Attribute

To access the value of an attribute, use the <samp class="listingcharacter">getAttribute()</samp> method on the respective element. As a parameter, the method expects the name of the respective HTML attribute. It then returns the value of the corresponding attribute. Use the HTML code from [Listing 5.34](#05_005.html_l5.34) as a starting point: it shows a link (an <samp class="listingcharacter"><a></samp> element) with the <samp class="listingcharacter">id</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">href</samp> attributes.

```
<a id="home" class="link" href="index.html">Home</a> 
```

**Listing 5.34**     An HTML Link

To access these attributes, use the <samp class="listingcharacter">getAttribute()</samp> method, as shown in [Listing 5.35](#05_005.html_l5.35).

```
const element = document.getElementById('home');
console.log(element.getAttribute('id'));    // home
console.log(element.getAttribute('class')); // link
console.log(element.getAttribute('href'));  // index.html 
```

**Listing 5.35**     You Can Access Attributes of an HTML Element Using the getAttribute() Method

The attributes of an element are usually also available as properties with the same name—although the <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> attribute is an exception: this attribute can be accessed via the <samp class="listingcharacter">className</samp> property. [Listing 5.36](#05_005.html_l5.36) shows a corresponding example: the <samp class="listingcharacter">id</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">href</samp> attributes can be read using the properties of the same name, the <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> attribute via the <samp class="listingcharacter">className</samp> property.

```
console.log(element.id);        // home
console.log(element.className); // link
console.log(element.href);      // index.html 
```

**Listing 5.36**     The Attributes of an Element Are Also Available as Properties

However, you should note the following: for two attributes, the access via the <samp class="listingcharacter">getAttribute()</samp> method returns a different return value than the direct access via the property. For the <samp class="listingcharacter">style</samp> attribute, the <samp class="listingcharacter">getAttribute()</samp> method only returns the text contained as a value in the attribute. The access to the <samp class="listingcharacter">style</samp> property, on the other hand, returns an object of the <samp class="listingcharacter">CSSStyleDeclaration</samp> type, which can be used to access the corresponding CSS information in detail. In addition, all attributes that can be used to define event handlers (see also [Chapter 6](#06_001.html_h6)) return the JavaScript code to be executed as a function object via the corresponding property (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">onclick</samp>). If, on the other hand, the respective attribute is accessed via the <samp class="listingcharacter">getAttribute()</samp> method, the name of the function to be executed is returned as text.

Take a look at [Listing 5.37](#05_005.html_l5.37) and [Listing 5.38](#05_005.html_l5.38). The former shows an HTML button with various attributes, including a <samp class="listingcharacter">style</samp> attribute and an <samp class="listingcharacter">onclick</samp> attribute. In the latter, you can then see how both are accessed via the property of the same name and via the <samp class="listingcharacter">getAttribute()</samp> method, respectively.

```
<button id="create" class="link" style="background-color: green" 
onclick="createContact()">Create contact</button> 
```

**Listing 5.37**     An HTML Button

```
const button = document.getElementById('create');
console.log(button.onclick);                        // Output of the 
                                                    // function object
console.log(typeof button.onclick);                 // Output: function
console.log(button.getAttribute('onclick'));        // createContact()
console.log(typeof button.getAttribute('onclick')); // Output: string
console.log(button.style);                          // Output of 
                                                    // CSSStyleDeclaration
console.log(typeof button.style);                   // Output: object
console.log(button.getAttribute('style'));          // background-color: green
console.log(typeof button.getAttribute('style'));   // Output: string 
```

**Listing 5.38**     Accessing Event Handlers and the style Attribute Returns Different Return Values Depending on the Access Type

The reason that direct access to event handler attributes like <samp class="listingcharacter">onclick</samp> doesn’t return a string but a function is that this property enables you to define event handlers for the respective element. That is, you can assign function objects to this property.

The reason that direct access to the <samp class="listingcharacter">style</samp> attribute doesn’t return a string is that this attribute can be used to programmatically access the CSS information of the respective element, even with write access (as you’ve already seen in this chapter).

### 5.5.2    Changing the Value of an Attribute or Adding a New Attribute

To change the value of an attribute or add a new attribute, use the <samp class="listingcharacter">setAttribute()</samp> method on the element for which the attribute is to be changed. This method expects two parameters: the name of the attribute and the new value. If the corresponding element already has an attribute of the same name, the value of that attribute will be overwritten with the new value. If the attribute doesn’t yet exist, a corresponding attribute is newly added to the element. An example is shown in [Listing 5.39](#05_005.html_l5.39). This listing changes the <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">href</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">target</samp> properties for the previously selected link element.

```
const element = document.getElementById('home');
element.setAttribute('class', 'link active');
element.setAttribute('href', 'newlink.html');
element.setAttribute('target', '_blank');
console.log(element.getAttribute('class'));   // link active
console.log(element.getAttribute('href'));    // newlink.html
console.log(element.getAttribute('target'));  // _blank 
```
