  const messageContainer = errorContainer.querySelector('.error-message');
  if(!emailElement.validity.valid) {
    messageContainer.textContent = emailElement.validationMessage;
    errorContainer.style.display = 'block';
  } else {
    messageContainer.textContent = '';
    errorContainer.style.display = 'none';
  }
}

document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', init); 
```

**Listing 7.23**     Checking if Two Input Fields Contain the Same Value

[![Example of a Validation That Cannot Be Implemented Using Only HTML](bilderklein/klein07_010.png)](img-f7.10.html)

**Figure 7.10**     Example of a Validation That Cannot Be Implemented Using Only HTML

[![Only if Both Email Fields Contain the Same Value Is the Validation Successful](bilderklein/klein07_011.png)](img-f7.11.html)

**Figure 7.11** Only if Both Email Fields Contain the Same Value Is the Validation Successful

If, on the other hand, you want to trigger the native validation with JavaScript only after a form has been submitted or the corresponding submit button has been pressed, you have to set the <samp class="listingcharacter">noValidate</samp> property to <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>, as shown in [Listing 7.24](#07_003.html_l7.24). By default, the native validation is performed before the submit event is triggered. This means that the browser's default outputs (including the standard validation messages) are displayed first, before you have the option to perform your own validations and generate customized outputs via JavaScript. But if you set the <samp class="listingcharacter">noValidate</samp> property to <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>, as in the example, you disable the browser's default output. (By the way, the rest of the code in the example ensures that all form elements of the form are checked for validity.)

```
function init() {
  const registerForm = document.getElementById('register');
  registerForm.noValidate = true; 
  registerForm.addEventListener('submit', validateForm);
}

document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', init);

function validateForm(e) {
  const event = (e ? e : window.event); // Event
  const form = (event.target            // Target element
            ? event.target
            : event.srcElement);
  let formIsValid = true;               // Validity of the form
  const formElements =                  // Form elements ...
    form.querySelectorAll(              // ... that support ...
      'input, textarea, select');       // ... native validation
  for (let i = 0; i < formElements.length; i++) {
    const formElement = formElements[i];
    if (formElement.willValidate !== 'undefined') {
      formElement.checkValidity();
    } else {
                                        // Browser does not support
                                        // native HTML5 validation.
    }
    if (!formElement.validity.valid) {  // If the value is not valid ...
      formIsValid = false;              // ... the form data is not valid.
    }
  }
  if (!formIsValid) {                   // If the form data is not valid ...
    if (event.preventDefault) {         // ...
      event.preventDefault();           // ... prevent default actions.
    }
  }
  return formIsValid;
} 
```

**Listing 7.24**     Validating All Form Fields within a Form

## 7.4    Summary

In this chapter, you learned how to work with forms. You learned how to read values from the different type of form elements, how to validate form data, and how to submit forms. The following are the most important points to remember from this chapter:

*   Forms within a web page can be selected in several ways: via the familiar DOM selection methods, via the <samp class="listingcharacter">forms</samp> property of the <samp class="listingcharacter">document</samp> object, and via properties of the <samp class="listingcharacter">document</samp> object that correspond to the name of the respective form.

*   To avoid having to modify your JavaScript code when making changes regarding the order of forms on a web page, you should usually use DOM selection methods such as <samp class="listingcharacter">getElementById()</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">querySelector()</samp> to select forms.

*   Individual form elements within a form can also be selected in different ways: via the DOM selection methods and via the <samp class="listingcharacter">elements</samp> property of the respective form.

*   Accessing the values of individual form elements is generally quite similar. The values of text fields, password fields, checkboxes, and radio buttons can be accessed via the <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp> property. In the case of the latter two, the <samp class="listingcharacter">checked</samp> property also can be used to check whether the respective element is selected or not.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">submit()</samp> method can be used to submit forms via JavaScript, while the <samp class="listingcharacter">reset()</samp> method resets them to their default values.

*   The Constraint Validation API is available for validating form inputs. Using this API, you can use the native HTML5 validations and perform your own validations.

# 8    Controlling Browsers and Reading Browser Information

In addition to the Document Object Model, which you learned about in [Chapter 5](#05_001.html_h5), browsers provide a second special object model that you can use to access browser-relevant information via JavaScript. In this chapter, we’ll use this model to show you how to access window information, how to influence the navigation panel and browsing history, and how to identify the browser.

In browser runtime environments, the Browser Object Model (BOM or BOM API) is available in addition to the DOM. Through this object model, it’s possible to control certain aspects of the browser (such as going back and forth in the browsing history) and to read certain information from the browser (such as information about the size and position of the current browser window).

## 8.1    The Browser Object Model

The entry point for the Browser Object Model is the global <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object, as shown in [Figure 8.1](#08_001.html_f8.1). This object represents a single browser window (or more precisely, a single browser tab as each browser tab contains its own object instance).

This global object is also the entry point to the Document Object Model (see [Chapter 5](#05_001.html_h5)), which, as you know, is represented by the <samp class="listingcharacter">document</samp> object. Strictly speaking, the latter is actually a property of the <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object, but it’s also implicitly provided as a global object by browsers (so you can write both <samp class="listingcharacter">document</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">window.document</samp>).

The standard JavaScript objects, like <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Array</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Function</samp>, which we discussed in [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4), are properties of the <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object as well, but they’re also available as global variables.

In addition, the <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object also provides the entry point to various HTML5 Web APIs—for example, the Geolocation API, the Storage API, and many more, which we’ll discuss in [Chapter 12](#12_001.html_h12).

[![Classification of the Browser Object Model](bilderklein/klein08_001.png)](img-f8.1.html)

**Figure 8.1** Classification of the Browser Object Model

In this chapter, however, we’ll only deal with the BOM API for the time being. Specifically, we’ll introduce the following five topics that result directly from the properties of the <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object:

*   First, there are some properties that contain concrete information regarding the browser window and methods that can be used to open various dialog boxes. We’ll discuss these properties and methods in [Section 8.2](#08_002.html_h8.2).

*   Secondly, the <samp class="listingcharacter">location</samp> property contains information about the current URL of the browser window ([Section 8.3](#08_003.html_h8.3)). This property allows you to access the various components of the current URL.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">history</samp> property contains a reference to an object of the <samp class="listingcharacter">History</samp> type. This allows you to access and modify the browsing history ([Section 8.4](#08_004.html_h8.4)).

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">navigator</samp> property contains a reference to an object of the <samp class="listingcharacter">navigator</samp> type. This object provides general information of the browser, like its name, manufacturer details, and so on ([Section 8.5](#08_005.html_h8.5)).

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">screen</samp> property contains a reference to an object of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Screen</samp> type, which you can use to retrieve information about the screen, like its height and width, color depth, pixel depth, and so on ([Section 8.6](#08_006.html_h8.6)).

###### Background Information

Strictly speaking, the <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object represents the global object defined in ECMAScript and thus also has all the properties (<samp class="listingcharacter">undefined</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">NaN</samp>, etc.) and methods (<samp class="listingcharacter">parseFloat()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">parseInt()</samp>, etc.) that are defined in the standard for this object and that you already learned about in [Chapter 3](#03_001.html_h3). The fact that the <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object represents the global object is, in turn, the reason that all properties and methods of the <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object are also available globally (and you don't always have to prepend <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> when accessing it).

## 8.2    Accessing Window Information

Let’s start by introducing the general properties of the <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object for accessing window information, as well as the methods provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object.

### 8.2.1    Determining the Size and Position of a Browser Window

To determine the size and position of a browser window, there is a whole set of properties that provide every conceivable dimension (see [Figure 8.2](#08_002.html_f8.2)). The <samp class="listingcharacter">outerHeight</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">outerWidth</samp> properties represent the height and width of the browser window, including all displayed browser bars. The <samp class="listingcharacter">innerHeight</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">innerWidth</samp> properties, on the other hand, represent the height and width without the browser bars, but including scrollbars.

[![Size and Position Information of a Browser Window (or Browser Tab)](bilderklein/klein08_002.png)](img-f8.2.html)

**Figure 8.2**     Size and Position Information of a Browser Window (or Browser Tab)

You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">screenX</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">screenY</samp> properties to find out where the browser window is located horizontally and vertically on the screen. You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">scrollX</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">scrollY</samp> properties to determine how far the content of the browser window has been scrolled horizontally and vertically (alternatively, simply use <samp class="listingcharacter">pageXOffset</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">pageYOffset</samp>). An overview of these properties can be found in [Table 8.1](#08_002.html_t8.1), and some examples are shown in [Listing 8.1](#08_002.html_l8.1).

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">innerHeight</samp> | Contains the height of the window content, including (if shown) the horizontal scrollbar but excluding other browser bars |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">innerWidth</samp> | Contains the width of the window content, including (if shown) the vertical scrollbar but excluding other browser bars |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">outerHeight</samp> | Contains the height of the browser window, including all browser bars |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">outerWidth</samp> | Contains the width of the browser window, including all browser bars |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">pageXOffset</samp> | An alias for <samp class="listingcharacter">window.scrollX</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">pageYOffset</samp> | An alias for <samp class="listingcharacter">window.scrollY</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">screenX</samp> | Contains the position of the browser window on the x-axis—in other words, the distance of the browser window from the left edge of the screen |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">screenY</samp> | Contains the position of the browser window on the y-axis—in other words, the distance of the browser window from the top of the screen |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">scrollX</samp> | Contains the number of pixels the web page has already been scrolled horizontally |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">scrollY</samp> | Contains the number of pixels the web page has already been scrolled vertically |

**Table 8.1**     Properties Relevant to Size and Position of the window Object

```
console.log(window.innerHeight);    // e.g. 600
console.log(window.innerWidth);     // e.g. 1134
console.log(window.screenX);        // e.g. 100
console.log(window.screenY);        // e.g. 22 
```

**Listing 8.1**     Determining the Size and Position of a Browser Window

You can also use the <samp class="listingcharacter">scrollX</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">scrollY</samp> properties (not shown in [Figure 8.2](#08_002.html_f8.2)) to determine how far the content of a web page has scrolled horizontally and vertically within the browser window. You saw an example of this in [Chapter 6](#06_001.html_h6), where we used the <samp class="listingcharacter">scrollY</samp> property to fade elements into the web page depending on the vertical scroll position.

### 8.2.2    Changing the Size and Position of a Browser Window

Of course, you can not only determine the size and position of a browser window, but also resize a browser window and change its position on the screen. For this purpose, the <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object offers various methods (see also [Listing 8.2](#08_002.html_l8.2)): The <samp class="listingcharacter">moveBy()</samp> method can be used to move a browser window horizontally and vertically by a specified number of pixels, and the <samp class="listingcharacter">moveTo()</samp> method can be used to move the window to a specific position. Via the <samp class="listingcharacter">resizeBy()</samp> method, you can scale a browser window by a certain factor, and via the <samp class="listingcharacter">resizeTo()</samp> method you can scale to a certain size. The <samp class="listingcharacter">scrollTo()</samp> method scrolls the window contents to a specified position, and the <samp class="listingcharacter">scrollBy()</samp> method scrolls the window contents by a specified horizontal and vertical number of pixels. An overview of all these methods can be found in [Table 8.2](#08_002.html_t8.2).

```
// Move browser window by 200 pixels both horizontally and vertically
window.moveBy(200, 200);
// Move browser window to position (200, 200)
window.moveTo(200, 200);
// Enlarge browser window by 200 pixels in width and height
window.resizeBy(200, 200);
// Shrink browser window by 200 pixels in width and height
window.resizeBy(-200, -200);
// Move browser content by 200 pixels both horizontally and vertically
window.scrollBy(200, 200);
// Move browser content to position (200, 200)
window.scrollTo(200, 200); 
```

**Listing 8.2**     Changing the Size and Position of a Browser Window

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">moveBy()</samp> | Moves the current browser window horizontally and vertically by a specified number of pixels. The first parameter determines the horizontal, the second parameter the vertical movement in pixels. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">moveTo()</samp> | Moves the current browser window horizontally and vertically to a specified position. The first parameter determines the horizontal, the second parameter the vertical position in pixels. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">resizeBy()</samp> | Scales the current browser window horizontally and vertically by a specified number of pixels. The first parameter determines the horizontal scaling value, the second parameter the vertical scaling value. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">resizeTo()</samp> | Scales the current browser window horizontally and vertically to a specified size. The first parameter determines the width, the second parameter the height. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">scroll()</samp> | Scrolls the window contents to a specified position. The first parameter indicates the horizontal position, the second parameter the vertical position. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">scrollBy()</samp> | Scrolls the window content by a specified factor. The first parameter specifies the horizontal scroll factor, the second parameter specifies the vertical scroll factor. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">scrollTo()</samp> | Scrolls the window contents to a specified position. The first parameter indicates the horizontal position, the second parameter the vertical position. |

**Table 8.2**     The Methods of the window Object to Define the Size and Position of the Browser Window and the Window Content

### 8.2.3    Accessing Display Information of the Browser Bars

A browser window typically consists of various components (see [Figure 8.3](#08_002.html_f8.3)). In addition to the content area that displays the web page, there is an address bar in which you can enter a URL (or in most modern browsers, also a search term, which then starts the preconfigured search engine); a status bar that indicates, among other things, whether a web page has been loaded or is in the process of being loaded; a menu bar; a toolbar; a "personal" bar (containing bookmarks, for example); and, last but not least, scrollbars, which display the horizontal and vertical position of the respective web page.

[![Structure of a Browser Window (or Browser Tab)](bilderklein/klein08_003.png)](img-f8.3.html)

**Figure 8.3**     Structure of a Browser Window (or Browser Tab)

You can find out whether these browser bars are displayed or not using the properties listed in [Table 8.3](#08_002.html_t8.3).

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">locationbar</samp> | Contains a reference to an object that provides information about whether the address bar is displayed or not |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">menubar</samp> | Contains a reference to an object that provides information about whether the menu bar is displayed or not |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">personalbar</samp> | Contains a reference to an object that provides information about whether the personal bar (e.g., the bookmark bar) is displayed or not |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">scrollbars</samp> | Contains a reference to an object that provides information about whether the scrollbars are displayed or not |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">statusbar</samp> | Contains a reference to an object that provides information about whether the status bar is displayed or not |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">toolbar</samp> | Contains a reference to an object that provides information about whether the toolbar is displayed or not |

**Table 8.3**     Properties of the window Object with Respect to the Various Browser Bars

### 8.2.4    Determining General Properties

In addition to the properties presented in the previous sections, there are a few more properties that we’ll briefly mention here (see [Table 8.4](#08_002.html_t8.4)). The <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> property, for example, contains the name of the browser window. This does not refer to the title of the loaded web page (which can be determined via <samp class="listingcharacter">document.title</samp>), but to a name that identifies the browser window as such (see also [Section 8.2.5](#08_002.html_h8.2.5)).

The <samp class="listingcharacter">opener</samp> property contains a reference to the browser window (object) from which the current browser window has been opened (again, [Section 8.2.5](#08_002.html_h8.2.5)). The <samp class="listingcharacter">self</samp> property, however, contains a reference to the <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object itself. If you want to access the current <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object within event listeners, this is particularly interesting to avoid conflicts with the <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> keyword.

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> | Contains the name of the window. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">opener</samp> | If you open a browser window from another browser window via JavaScript ([Section 8.2.5](#08_002.html_h8.2.5)), this property contains a reference to the original window. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">self</samp> | Contains a reference to an object representing the current browser window. |

**Table 8.4**     General Properties of the window Object

### 8.2.5    Opening New Browser Windows

The <samp class="listingcharacter">open()</samp> method is available for opening a new browser window. An example of this is shown in [Listing 8.3](#08_002.html_l8.3). The first argument you pass to the method is the URL of the web page that you want to open in the new window. As a second argument, you can optionally specify the name of the new window (not to be confused with the name of the web page). In addition, the third argument gives you the possibility to influence the appearance and behavior of the window. You can pass a string consisting of the properties shown in [Table 8.5](#08_002.html_t8.5). The value of the respective property is directly appended to the property using an equal sign; several property-value pairs are separated by commas.

In [Listing 8.3](#08_002.html_l8.3), for example, a browser window is created with a width of 500 pixels (<samp class="listingcharacter">width</samp> property) and a height of 500 pixels (<samp class="listingcharacter">height</samp> property), which is resizable (<samp class="listingcharacter">resizable</samp> property) and has scrollbars and a status bar (<samp class="listingcharacter">scrollbars</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">status</samp> properties). For the latter properties, and generally for those properties that can take only one of two states, the allowed values are <samp class="listingcharacter">yes</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">no</samp> (in the <samp class="listingcharacter">resizable</samp> example) and <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> (in the <samp class="listingcharacter">scrollbars</samp> example). Alternatively, the value can be omitted, in which case the presence of the property name is evaluated as <samp class="listingcharacter">yes</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> (in the <samp class="listingcharacter">status</samp> example).

```
const linkOpen = document.getElementById('link-open');
linkOpen.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const url = document.getElementById('url').value;
  window.open(
    url,                  // URL to open
    'Window title',       // Name of the window
    'width=500,' +        // Width of the window
    'height=500,' +       // Height of the window
    'resizable=yes,' +    // Resizing possible
    'scrollbars=1,' +     // Scrollbar enabled
    'status'              // Status bar enabled
  );
}); 
```

**Listing 8.3**     Opening a Browser Window

| Parameter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">height</samp> | The height of the new browser window in pixels |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">innerHeight</samp> | The height of the display area of the new browser window in pixels |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">innerWidth</samp> | The width of the display area of the new browser window in pixels |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">left</samp> | Distance of the upper left corner of the new browser window to the left edge of the screen in pixels |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">location</samp> | Indication of whether the new browser window should have an address bar or not |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">menubar</samp> | Indication of whether the new browser window should have a menu bar or not |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">resizable</samp> | Indication of whether the new browser window is resizable or not |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">screenX</samp> | Distance of the upper left corner of the new browser window to the left edge of the screen in pixels |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">screenY</samp> | Distance of the upper left corner of the new browser window to the top of the screen in pixels |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">scrollbars</samp> | Indication of whether the new browser window should have a scrollbar or not |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">status</samp> | Indication of whether the new browser window should have a status bar or not |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">toolbar</samp> | Indication of whether the new browser window should have a toolbar or not |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">top</samp> | Distance of the upper left corner of the new browser window to the top of the screen in pixels |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">width</samp> | The width of the new browser window in pixels |

**Table 8.5**     Selected Parameters for Opening Browser Windows

### 8.2.6    Closing the Browser Window

Analogous to the <samp class="listingcharacter">open()</samp> method, you can also use the <samp class="listingcharacter">close()</samp> method to close a browser window again. [Listing 8.4](#08_002.html_l8.4) shows an example that extends the previous example with a button (<samp class="listingcharacter">linkClose</samp>). In the event listener for the <samp class="listingcharacter">linkOpen</samp> button, the open browser window is saved (you can see that the <samp class="listingcharacter">open()</samp> method returns an object representing the open browser window). Inside the event listener for the <samp class="listingcharacter">linkClose</samp> button, the <samp class="listingcharacter">close()</samp> method is called on this object, closing the previously opened browser window again.

```
const windowReference;
const linkOpen = document.getElementById('link-open');
const linkClose = document.getElementById('link-close');
linkOpen.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const url = document.getElementById('url').value;
  windowReference = window.open(
    url,
    'Window title',
    'width=500,height=500,resizable,scrollbars=yes,status=1'
  );
});
linkClose.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  windowReference.close();
}); 
```

**Listing 8.4**     Closing a Browser Window

###### Opening the Browser Window via JavaScript

Although we just showed you how it works, we advise against opening browser windows via JavaScript. Such windows always have the negative connotation of annoying advertising windows. They are ignored by most browsers by default and not opened until users have given their consent.

### 8.2.7    Opening Dialogs

In addition to the methods presented so far for opening and closing browser windows, the <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object offers further methods (for a small selection, see [Table 8.6](#08_002.html_t8.6)). You already know about three of them from the previous chapters: you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">alert()</samp> method to open alert dialogs, the <samp class="listingcharacter">confirm()</samp> method to open confirmation dialogs, and the <samp class="listingcharacter">prompt()</samp> method to open dialogs in which you can enter text.

In addition, the <samp class="listingcharacter">find()</samp> method can be used to search for text within a web page, and the <samp class="listingcharacter">print()</samp> method can be used to print the contents of the current web page (see [Figure 8.4](#08_002.html_f8.4)).

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">alert()</samp> | Opens a dialog with a message |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">close()</samp> | Closes the browser window ([Section 8.2.6](#08_002.html_h8.2.6)) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">confirm()</samp> | Opens a dialog with a message |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">find()</samp> | Searches for a string in the browser window |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">open()</samp> | Creates a new browser window ([Section 8.2.5](#08_002.html_h8.2.5)) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">print()</samp> | Opens a dialog for printing the window contents |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">prompt()</samp> | Opens a dialog that allows users to enter text |

**Table 8.6**     Methods of the window Object for Opening Dialogs

[![The print() Method Opens the Dialog for Printing the Current Web Page](bilderklein/klein08_004.png)](img-f8.4.html)

**Figure 8.4** The print() Method Opens the Dialog for Printing the Current Web Page

### 8.2.8    Executing Functions in a Time-Controlled Manner

If you want to execute certain functions within a web page with a delay (once) or at certain intervals (repeatedly), the <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object provides several helper methods for this purpose (see also [Table 8.7](#08_002.html_t8.7)).

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">setInterval()</samp> | Executes a function at specified time intervals. Returns an ID that can be passed as a parameter to the <samp class="listingcharacter">clearInterval()</samp> method to abort the execution of the function. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">clearInterval()</samp> | Cancels the execution of the function triggered by <samp class="listingcharacter">setInterval()</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">setTimeout()</samp> | Executes a function after a specified period of time. Returns an ID that can be passed as a parameter to the <samp class="listingcharacter">clearTimeout()</samp> method to prevent the function from executing. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">clearTimeout()</samp> | Cancels the execution of the function triggered by <samp class="listingcharacter">setTimeout()</samp>. |

**Table 8.7**     Methods of the window Object for the Time-Controlled Execution of Functions

The <samp class="listingcharacter">setTimeout()</samp> method can be used to define after what time period a certain function should be executed. As the first argument, you pass an anonymous function or the name of the corresponding function, and as the second argument the time period in milliseconds after which the function should be executed. Some examples are shown in [Listing 8.5](#08_002.html_l8.5). The first call of <samp class="listingcharacter">setTimeout()</samp> passes an anonymous function, the second call passes an (anonymous) arrow function, and the third call passes the <samp class="listingcharacter">printMessage()</samp> function. All three calls ensure that after 5,000 milliseconds (i.e., after five seconds), the passed function is executed and the message <samp class="listingcharacter">Hello World</samp> is output to the console.

```
window.setTimeout(function() {
  console.log('Hello World');
}, 5000);

window.setTimeout(() => {
  console.log('Hello World');
}, 5000);
function printMessage() {
  console.log('Hello World');
}
window.setTimeout(printMessage, 5000); 
```

**Listing 8.5**     Executing a Function after Five Seconds

Analogous to the <samp class="listingcharacter">setTimout()</samp> method, the <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object provides the <samp class="listingcharacter">setInterval()</samp> method, which can be used to execute a function at specific time intervals. As the first argument, you pass either an anonymous function or the name of the function to be executed, and as the second argument the interval in milliseconds at which the function is to be executed. [Listing 8.6](#08_002.html_l8.6) shows some examples. All three calls to <samp class="listingcharacter">setInterval()</samp> cause the passed function to be executed every 5,000 milliseconds.

```
window.setInterval(function() {
  console.log('Hello World');
}, 5000);

window.setInterval(() => {
  console.log('Hello World');
}, 5000);
function printMessage() {
  console.log('Hello World');
}
window.setInterval(printMessage, 5000); 
```

**Listing 8.6**     Executing a Function Every Five Seconds

## 8.3    Accessing Navigation Information of a Currently Open Web Page

Using the object stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter">location</samp> property (which is of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Location</samp> type), you can access information regarding the URL of the web page currently loaded in the browser window or tab.

### 8.3.1    Accessing the Individual Components of the URL

A URL consists of different components, as shown in [Figure 8.5](#08_003.html_f8.5). Among other things, a URL consists of a protocol, the host name, a port specification, a path specification, and query parameters. The properties to access the individual components of a URL are listed in [Table 8.8](#08_003.html_t8.8).

[![The Components of a URL](bilderklein/klein08_005.png)](img-f8.5.html)

**Figure 8.5**     The Components of a URL

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">href</samp> | Contains the entire URL. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">protocol</samp> | Contains the protocol of the URL including the colon, e.g. <samp class="listingcharacter">https:</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">host</samp> | Contains the hostname of a URL—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">javascripthandbuch.de</samp>. If a port specification is available, it will also be listed—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">philipackermann.de:8080</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">hostname</samp> | Contains the domain of a URL—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">javascripthandbuch.de</samp>. Unlike the <samp class="listingcharacter">host</samp> property, <samp class="listingcharacter">hostname</samp> does not include a port specification. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">port</samp> | Contains the port of a URL—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">8080</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">pathname</samp> | Contains the path of a URL, starting with a <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">search</samp> | Contains the parameters of a URL—that is, the query string (also search string)—including a preceding question mark—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">?firstName=John</samp>. Multiple parameter-value pairs are separated by an ampersand symbol—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">?firstName=John&lastName=Doe</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">hash</samp> | Contains the fragment identifier, including a preceding <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp>. In the case of the URL <samp class="listingcharacter">http://www.javascripthandbuch.de#services</samp>, this would be <samp class="listingcharacter">#services</samp>. If you call a URL with a fragment identifier and there is an element with the corresponding ID on the respective web page, the display area is scrolled to this element. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">username</samp> | Contains the username specified in the URL. For the URL <samp class="listingcharacter">https://john:secret@javascripthandbuch.de</samp>, this would be the value <samp class="listingcharacter">john</samp>. Not supported by all browsers. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">password</samp> | Contains the password specified in the URL. For the URL <samp class="listingcharacter">https://max:secret@javascripthandbuch.de</samp>, this would be the value <samp class="listingcharacter">secret</samp>. Not supported by all browsers. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">origin</samp> | Contains the canonical form of the URL, consisting of the protocol, followed by <samp class="listingcharacter">://</samp>, the domain, and—if the URL contains a port specification—a colon and the port specification. |

**Table 8.8**     The Properties of Location

### 8.3.2    Accessing Query String Parameters

Unfortunately, there is no method available for accessing the individual parameters in the query string of a URL. Instead, you have to parse the query string itself or use a helper function, as shown in [Listing 8.7](#08_003.html_l8.7). This function expects the name of the parameter for which the value is to be determined, creates a regular expression using this parameter, and extracts the value for the parameter (if available) from the query string of the URL (<samp class="listingcharacter">location.search</samp>).

```
function getParameterByName(name) {
  name = name.replace(/[\[]/, '\\[').replace(/[\]]/, '\\]');
  const regex = new RegExp('[\\?&]' + name + '=([^&#]*)'),
    results = regex.exec(location.search);
  return results === null ? '' : decodeURIComponent(results[1].replace(/\+/g, ' '));
}
console.log(getParameterByName('tests')); 
```

**Listing 8.7**     Helper Function for Extracting Individual Query String Parameters

### 8.3.3    Loading a New Web Page

To load a new web page in the current browser window, you have several options.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">assign()</samp> method expects a URL as argument and opens the corresponding web page. This also creates a new entry in the browsing history. You can see an example of this in [Listing 8.8](#08_003.html_l8.8).

```
const linkLoad = document.getElementById('link-load');
linkLoad.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const url = document.getElementById('url').value;
  window.location.assign(url);
}); 
```

**Listing 8.8**     Loading a Web Page via the assign() Method

Basically, the <samp class="listingcharacter">replace()</samp> method works in the same way as the <samp class="listingcharacter">assign()</samp> method: the URL of the web page to be loaded is passed as an argument (see [Listing 8.9](#08_003.html_l8.9)). Unlike <samp class="listingcharacter">assign()</samp>, however, calling <samp class="listingcharacter">replace()</samp> doesn’t result in a new entry being created in the browsing history. So in this case, you can no longer navigate back to the previously visited website.

```
const linkLoad = document.getElementById('link-load');
linkLoad.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const url = document.getElementById('url').value;
  window.location.replace(url);
}); 
```

**Listing 8.9**     Loading a Web Page Using the replace() Method

In addition, the <samp class="listingcharacter">href</samp> property of the <samp class="listingcharacter">location</samp> object can also be used to load a new web page, as shown in [Listing 8.10](#08_003.html_l8.10).

```
const linkLoad = document.getElementById('link-load');
linkLoad.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const url = document.getElementById('url').value;
  window.location.href = url;
}); 
```

**Listing 8.10**     Loading a Web Page Using the href Property

If you want to reload the current web page, you can do this using the <samp class="listingcharacter">reload()</samp> method. Optionally, a Boolean value can be passed to the method to determine whether the web page should be reloaded from the server (in this case, pass the value <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>) or whether the browser can also reload the web page from its internal cache (in this case, pass the value <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>). An example of this is shown in [Listing 8.11](#08_003.html_l8.11).

```
const linkReload = document.getElementById('link-reload');
linkReload.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  window.location.reload(true);
}); 
```

**Listing 8.11**     Reloading a Web Page via the reload() Method

## 8.4    Viewing and Modifying the Browsing History

The <samp class="listingcharacter">history</samp> property of the <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object takes you to an object that represents the browsing history. This object (of the <samp class="listingcharacter">History</samp> type) can be used to take a look at the history, but it can also enable you to change the history.

### 8.4.1    Navigating in the Browsing History

Each time the browser loads a new web page, or even jumps to a jump label (an anchor) within a web page, the browser creates a new entry in the browsing history by default (the exception here is the <samp class="listingcharacter">replace()</samp> method, as shown in [Section 8.3.3](#08_003.html_h8.3.3)).

A few years ago, it wasn’t so easy to influence the browsing history. The only things you could do (and still can do) were use the <samp class="listingcharacter">length</samp> property to see the number of entries in the browsing history, the <samp class="listingcharacter">back()</samp> method to go back one entry, the <samp class="listingcharacter">forward()</samp> method to go forward one entry, and the <samp class="listingcharacter">go()</samp> method to go to a specific entry in the browsing history (see [Table 8.9](#08_004.html_t8.9)). Some examples are shown in [Listing 8.12](#08_004.html_l8.12).

```
window.history.length;     // number of entries
window.history.back();     // back in history
window.history.forward();  // forward in history
window.history.go(-2);     // two entries back
window.history.go(2);      // two entries forward
window.history.go(0);      // reload current web page 
```

**Listing 8.12**     Access to the Browsing History

| Property/Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">length</samp> | Contains the number of entries in the history, including the currently loaded web page. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">back()</samp> | Goes to the previous web page in the history. Identical to the user pressing the browser's Back button. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">forward()</samp> | Goes to the following web page in the history. Identical to the user pressing the browser's Next button. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">go()</samp> | Goes to a specific web page in the history. The method is passed the increment starting from the current web page. For example, the value <samp class="listingcharacter">-1</samp> causes the previous web page to be opened, and the value <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> causes the following web page to be opened. If a value is passed for which there is no corresponding web page in the history, this method does nothing. If, on the other hand, the method is called without a value or with the value <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>, the current web page is reloaded. |

**Table 8.9**     The Old Properties and Methods of History That Are Still Valid

### 8.4.2    Browsing History for Single-Page Applications

However, with the success of single-page applications, where only parts of a web page/application are reloaded, a new or additional functionality was needed to describe individual entries in the browsing history. The reason: if only parts of a web page are reloaded, the URL doesn’t change by default, so there is no new entry in the browsing history. Bookmarking then isn’t possible either because different web pages (or more precisely, different states of a web page) don’t have their own URLs.

Therefore, the fragment identifier of the URL was used for a long time (see <samp class="listingcharacter">hash</samp> property in [Table 8.8](#08_003.html_t8.8)). If parts of a web page were reloaded, you simply changed this fragment identifier and thus ensured that a new entry was created in the browsing history.

Here's a quick example: Suppose you were visiting a web page with the URL www.javascripthandbuch.de that has five different navigation entries: Home, Services, Skills, About Us, and Contact. The individual URLs would then be www.javascripthandbuch.de#home, www.javascripthandbuch.de#services, www.javascripthandbuch.de#skills, www.javascripthandbuch.de#aboutus, and www.javascripthandbuch.de#contact. Such URLs are also called hashbang URLs because of the # character they contain (see [Listing 8.13](#08_004.html_l8.13)).

```
...
<body>
  <nav>
    <ul>
      <li><a href="#home">Home</a></li>
      <li><a href="#services">Services</a></li>
      <li><a href="#skills">Skills</a></li>
      <li><a href="#aboutus">About Us</a></li>
      <li><a href="#contact">Contact</a></li>
    </ul>
  </nav>
  <main id="content"></main>
</body>
... 
```

**Listing 8.13**     Hashbang URLs

But this technique isn’t ideal; it has some limitations. For example, the fragment identifier is only available on the client side and is not sent to the server.

### 8.4.3    Adding Entries to the Browsing History

For some time now, several adjustments have therefore been available (within the framework of the History API) that make it easier to work with the browsing history in the previously mentioned cases as well. The API defines a new property and two new methods for this purpose: the <samp class="listingcharacter">state</samp> property contains the current entry in the browsing history, the <samp class="listingcharacter">pushState()</samp> method can be used to place a new entry in the history, and the <samp class="listingcharacter">replaceState()</samp> method can be used to replace the current entry (see [Table 8.10](#08_004.html_t8.10)).

| Property/Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">state</samp> | Contains the current entry in the browsing history. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">pushState()</samp> | Adds an entry to the history. Any JavaScript object (the so-called state object), the title, and optionally a URL are passed. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">replaceState()</samp> | Replaces the current entry in the history with a new entry. A state object, the title, and optionally a URL are passed. |

**Table 8.10**     The Newer Properties and Methods of History

Let me demonstrate the use of these methods by adapting the previous example. First, hashbang URLs aren’t used. Instead, normal URLs are used, as shown in the HTML code in [Listing 8.14](#08_004.html_l8.14). The goal is not to load a new web page when one of the links is clicked, but to update the content in the <samp class="listingcharacter"><main></samp> element while still creating a new entry in the browsing history.

```
...
<body>
  <nav>
    <ul>
      <li><a href="/home">Home</a></li>
      <li><a href="/services">Services</a></li>
      <li><a href="/skills">Skills</a></li>
      <li><a href="/aboutus">About Us</a></li>
      <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
    </ul>
  </nav>
  <main id="content"></main>
</body>
... 
```

**Listing 8.14**     No Hashbang URLs Are Required when Using the New History API

[Listing 8.15](#08_004.html_l8.15) shows the corresponding JavaScript code. For each link on the web page, an event listener is registered that calls the <samp class="listingcharacter">pushState()</samp> method, adding a new entry to the browsing history. The first argument passed here is the content to be displayed, which for simplicity is contained in the <samp class="listingcharacter">contents</samp> object (in practice, the content would be dynamically loaded from the server instead; see also [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9)).

The second parameter passed is the title to be displayed in the browser title bar when the corresponding link is clicked. For this purpose, the text content of the respective link element is used (<samp class="listingcharacter">event.target.textContent</samp>). Finally, the third parameter is the URL to be displayed in the address bar. Here, the content of the <samp class="listingcharacter">href</samp> attribute of the corresponding link element is used (<samp class="listingcharacter">event.target.href</samp>).

Calling <samp class="listingcharacter">preventDefault()</samp> on the event object also prevents the default action from being executed when the links are clicked. If you omitted this call, the browser would simply reload the URL of the link.

```
function init() {
  // Container element for the content
  const contentElement = document.getElementById('content');
  // Sample content, normally loaded via Ajax
  const contents = {
      home: {
        content: 'Home'
      },
      services: {
        content: 'Services'
      },
      skills: {
        content: 'Skills'
      },
      aboutus: {
        content: 'About Us'
      },
      contact: {
        content: 'Contact'
      }
    };
  // Event listener for the links
  function handleClick(event) {
    const pageName = event.target.getAttribute('href').split('/').pop();
    const content = contents[pageName];
    updateContent(content.content);
    history.pushState(
      content,  // State object
      event.target.textContent,   // Title
      event.target.href           // URL
    );
    return event.preventDefault();
  }
  // Register the event listeners
  const linkElements = document.getElementsByTagName('a');
  for (let i = 0; i < linkElements.length; i++) {
    linkElements[i].addEventListener('click', handleClick, true);
  }
  function updateContent(content) {
    contentElement.textContent = content;
  }
}

document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', init); 
```

**Listing 8.15**     Adding Entries to the Browsing History

###### Web Servers

The code in [Listing 8.15](#08_004.html_l8.15) only works when the HTML is run through a web server, not when it’s opened as a local file.

### 8.4.4    Responding to Changes in the Browsing History

Every time the current entry in the browsing history changes (e.g., when you press the Back button in the browser), the <samp class="listingcharacter">popstate</samp> event is triggered. At the moment (i.e., only with the source code from [Listing 8.15](#08_004.html_l8.15)), however, the content of the web page is not yet updated because the <samp class="listingcharacter">updateContent()</samp> method is only called when one of the links is clicked, not when the Back button is used (and also not when the Next button is clicked).

To achieve this and update the content of the <samp class="listingcharacter"><main></samp> element even when using the browser buttons, you simply need to call the <samp class="listingcharacter">updateContent()</samp> method inside an event listener for the <samp class="listingcharacter">popstate</samp> event (see [Listing 8.16](#08_004.html_l8.16)).

The event listener is passed an event object of the <samp class="listingcharacter">PopStateEvent</samp> type, the <samp class="listingcharacter">state</samp> property of which gives you access to the entry removed from the browsing history. In the example, its <samp class="listingcharacter">content</samp> property is read and added to the container element for the content.

```
window.addEventListener('popstate', (event) => {
  updateContent(event.state.content);
}); 
```

**Listing 8.16**     Responding to Remote Entries in the Browsing History

### 8.4.5    Replacing the Current Entry in the Browsing History

To replace the current entry in the browsing history with another entry, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">replaceState()</samp> method. Like the <samp class="listingcharacter">pushState()</samp> method, this method is passed the state object, the name, and optionally a URL (see [Listing 8.17](#08_004.html_l8.17)).

```
history.replaceState(
  {
    content: contentElement.textContent
  },
  document.title,
  document.location.href
); 
```

**Listing 8.17**     Replacing an Entry in the Browsing History

You can see the connection between browsing history and the <samp class="listingcharacter">pushState()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">replaceState()</samp> methods in [Figure 8.6](#08_004.html_f8.6) (where, for the sake of clarity, the respective entries are only represented by the URL instead of showing the complete information, including the state object).

[![Difference between pushState() and replaceState() Methods](bilderklein/klein08_006.png)](img-f8.6.html)

**Figure 8.6**     Difference between pushState() and replaceState() Methods

## 8.5    Recognizing Browsers and Determining Browser Features

So far, you’ve seen how you can access and partially change information tied to the browser window, the current URL, and the browsing history. But if you want to access general browser information (browser name, browser manufacturer, etc.), use the <samp class="listingcharacter">navigator</samp> property of the <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object.

The object of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Navigator</samp> type stored in this property provides all sorts of such information (see [Table 8.11](#08_005.html_t8.11)), but some of it should be treated with caution or is marked as obsolete and should no longer be used.

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">appCodeName</samp> | Contains the internal codename of the current browser (not reliable, because every browser returns the value <samp class="listingcharacter">Mozilla</samp>). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">appName</samp> | Contains the official name of the current browser (not reliable, because every browser outputs the value <samp class="listingcharacter">Netscape</samp>). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">appVersion</samp> | Contains the version number of the current browser (not reliable). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">battery</samp> | Contains a reference to an object of the <samp class="listingcharacter">BatteryManager</samp> type that provides the entry point to the Battery Status API (see [Chapter 12](#12_001.html_h12)). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">cookieEnabled</samp> | Contains an indication of whether cookies are enabled or not. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">geolocation</samp> | Contains a reference to an object of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Geolocation</samp> type, which provides the entry point to the Geolocation API (see [Chapter 12](#12_001.html_h12)). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">language</samp> | Contains a string indicating the user's preferred language. Typically, this is the language that’s also used within the interface of the respective browser. If no preferred language could be determined, this property contains the value <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">languages</samp> | Contains a list of strings indicating the user's preferred languages, with the most preferred language in the first position (which corresponds to the language contained in the <samp class="listingcharacter">language</samp> property). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">mimeTypes</samp> | Contains a list of information about MIME types supported by the browser. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">onLine</samp> | Boolean indicating whether the browser is connected to the internet or not. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">platform</samp> | Contains information about the operating system used (not reliable). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">plugins</samp> | Contains a list of information about plug-ins that are supported by the browser. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">product</samp> | Contains the product name of the current browser. However, for backward compatibility, this returns the value <samp class="listingcharacter">Gecko</samp> in each browser. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">productSub</samp> | Contains the sublabel of the current browser (either <samp class="listingcharacter">20030107</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">20100101</samp>). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">serviceWorker</samp> | Contains a reference to an object of the <samp class="listingcharacter">ServiceWorkerContainer</samp> type, which provides the entry point to the Service Worker API. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">userAgent</samp> | Contains a string that identifies the browser used. However, it should be used with caution (see next note box). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">vendor</samp> | Contains information about the browser manufacturer (one of the values <samp class="listingcharacter">Apple Computer, Inc.</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Google Inc.</samp>, or an empty string). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">vendorSub</samp> | Actually intended for further information about the browser manufacturer, but always contains an empty string. |

**Table 8.11**     Properties of the navigator Object

For example, some time ago the <samp class="listingcharacter">navigator</samp> object was often used to draw conclusions about the browser used via the <samp class="listingcharacter">userAgent</samp> property in order to determine which features are supported by the browser and to execute the corresponding JavaScript code depending on this information. This technique is called browser detection or browser sniffing.

But today, browsers no longer use unique values for this property, so it’s no longer possible to draw conclusions about the browser used. For example, the property in Chrome returns the value <samp class="listingcharacter">Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 10_8_5) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/47.0.2526.111 Safari/537.36</samp>, which is anything but unique because it already contains different browser names.

This is also why browser detection technique is no longer used to draw conclusions about supported features. Instead, so-called feature detection directly searches for a feature. In other words, the specific browser used is usually not relevant for you as a web developer; more important is what features are supported by this browser.

For example, you can assume that a browser supports the new History API if the <samp class="listingcharacter">history</samp> object has a <samp class="listingcharacter">pushState()</samp> method (see [Listing 8.18](#08_005.html_l8.18)). So in feature detection, you directly test whether certain JavaScript objects have certain properties or methods that are indicative of the corresponding feature.

```
if(window.history.pushState) {
  // History API supported
} else {
  // History API not supported
} 
```

**Listing 8.18**     Feature Detection Example

###### Note

To check whether a browser supports a particular feature, you shouldn’t use the <samp class="listingcharacter">userAgent</samp> property of the <samp class="listingcharacter">navigator</samp> object; it’s considered very unreliable. Instead, you should use the feature detection technique.

## 8.6    Accessing Screen Information

The object stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter">screen</samp> property (of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Screen</samp> type) contains information related to the screen. These include the height (<samp class="listingcharacter">height</samp>) and width (<samp class="listingcharacter">width</samp>) of the screen, the color depth (<samp class="listingcharacter">colorDepth</samp>), and some information about how much space is available horizontally and vertically on the screen minus the fixed screen components (such as taskbars). [Figure 8.7](#08_006.html_f8.7) illustrates these properties, and you can find an overview in [Table 8.12](#08_006.html_t8.12).

[![Properties of the Screen Window](bilderklein/klein08_007.png)](img-f8.7.html)

**Figure 8.7**     Properties of the Screen Window

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">availTop</samp> | Contains a pixel value that indicates how much space is taken up from the top by fixed screen components such as taskbars and the like. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">availLeft</samp> | Contains a pixel value that indicates how much space is taken up from the left by fixed screen components such as taskbars and the like. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">availHeight</samp> | Contains the maximum available screen height in pixels minus the height of components like, for example, taskbars that are always displayed |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">availWidth</samp> | Contains the maximum available screen width in pixels minus the width of components like, for example, taskbars that are always displayed |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">colorDepth</samp> | Contains the color depth of the screen |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">height</samp> | Contains the height of the screen in pixels |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">orientation</samp> | Contains a reference to an object of the <samp class="listingcharacter">ScreenOrientation</samp> type, which provides information about the orientation of the screen and is a part of the Screen Orientation API ([http://www.w3.org/TR/screen-orientation](http://www.w3.org/TR/screen-orientation)) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">pixelDepth</samp> | Contains the pixel depth of the screen |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">width</samp> | Contains the width of the screen in pixels |

**Table 8.12**     Properties of the screen Object

## 8.7    Summary

In this chapter, you learned about the Browser Object Model, the object model through which you can access various components of the browser:

*   The global <samp class="listingcharacter">window</samp> object represents the entry point into the BOM.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">location</samp> object can be used to access components of the current URL and to reload web pages.

*   Using the <samp class="listingcharacter">history</samp> object, you can navigate the browsing history and create new entries in the browsing history.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">navigator</samp> object gives you detailed information about the browser, but not all of it is always reliable.

*   Via the <samp class="listingcharacter">screen</samp> object, you get information regarding the screen, like height and width, as well as color depth, pixel depth, and so on.

# 9    Dynamically Reloading Contents of a Web Page

For user interaction and in terms of user-friendliness, the concept of Ajax has become indispensable in the development of modern web applications. This technique enables you to dynamically update individual parts of a web page with content from the server instead of completely reloading the page.

In this chapter, we’ll show you how to dynamically reload or replace parts of a web page without reloading the entire web page. The technology behind this is called Ajax (Asynchronous JavaScript and XML).

## 9.1    The Principle of Ajax

The name Ajax was first coined in 2005 by Jesse James Garrett in his essay "A New Approach to Web Applications." The idea is to use JavaScript for exchanging data with the server in the background without completely reloading the web page itself.

### 9.1.1    Synchronous Communication

Let's first look at how the classic communication between client and server works via Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP). The client (usually the browser) sends a request (HTTP request) to the server, which then evaluates it and returns a corresponding response (HTTP response) to the client.

In terms of web page loading, this means that every time the user clicks on a link or fills out a form, for example, a corresponding HTTP request is sent to the server, which then generates the content of the new web page and returns it to the client (see [Figure 9.1](#09_001.html_f9.1)).

The less than ideal aspect of this process is that the client or browser has to wait while the server evaluates the request and prepares the response. As a user, you’ll notice this because you’ll no longer be able to interact with the website during this time; that is, no further requests can be made during the waiting time. For this reason, this type of communication, the orderly interplay between starting a request and waiting for the response, is also called synchronous communication.

[![The Principle of Synchronous Communication](bilderklein/klein09_001.png)](img-f9.1.html)

**Figure 9.1** The Principle of Synchronous Communication

To use a more illustrative example, let's look at the implementation of a classic search function within a web page. A search form is used to enter the criteria for the search, and then the form is submitted. The server evaluates the search request, usually performs one or more database queries, and creates the web page containing the search results (see [Figure 9.2](#09_001.html_f9.2)). While the server is doing this, the user can do nothing but wait for the results. Only when all search results have been determined and the response has been loaded from the server can the user continue the interaction—for example, browse through the search results in the overview or view each result in detail.

[![Sequence of a Synchronously Implemented Search](bilderklein/klein09_002.png)](img-f9.2.html)

**Figure 9.2**     Sequence of a Synchronously Implemented Search

### 9.1.2    Asynchronous Communication

When using Ajax, the communication takes place asynchronously, not synchronously, which is why this is referred to as asynchronous communication. Like with synchronous communication, first a complete web page is loaded from the server, or the client makes a request to the server, which processes it and delivers an appropriate response. Unlike synchronous communication, however, asynchronous communication also enables you to send new requests to the server while you are still waiting for the response to requests that have already been sent (see [Figure 9.3](#09_001.html_f9.3)). This makes it possible, for example, to independently update individual parts of a web page with data from the server.

[![The Principle of Asynchronous Communication](bilderklein/klein09_003.png)](img-f9.3.html)

**Figure 9.3** The Principle of Asynchronous Communication

If we apply this to the search example, then after submitting the search form, the form would be hidden, a progress bar would be displayed, and—after the search was completed—the search results would be displayed (see [Figure 9.4](#09_001.html_f9.4)). The other (fixed) components of the web page, such as the header, navigation, and footer areas, are not reloaded.

[![Workflow of an Asynchronous Search Implementation](bilderklein/klein09_004.png)](img-f9.4.html)

**Figure 9.4**     Workflow of an Asynchronous Search Implementation

This has some advantages: First, the data for the fixed components are not retransmitted from the server, which has an overall positive effect on the transmission time. Second, users have the possibility to continue interacting with other components on the website. For example, search results could be retrieved from the server piece by piece instead of all at once. A user could already view part of the search results, call detailed views of the results, and so on, while more search results were gradually retrieved from the server.

###### Note

Overall, asynchronous communication can significantly improve the user-friendliness and usability of a web page (or web application).

Technically, of course, HTTP requests are still sent during asynchronous communication as well. The only difference is that these are not triggered directly by the browser but are controlled via JavaScript calls (although synchronous calls are also possible using JavaScript, but more on that later).

The difference is illustrated once again in [Figure 9.5](#09_001.html_f9.5). Without Ajax (left side in the diagram), the HTTP requests are executed directly by the browser, but when using Ajax (right side in the diagram), this is done by the corresponding JavaScript code. The JavaScript code also handles processing the response from the server—for example, to update the user interface accordingly.

[![Difference between Classic and AJAX-Based Web Applications](bilderklein/klein09_005.png)](img-f9.5.html)

**Figure 9.5**     Difference between Classic and AJAX-Based Web Applications

### 9.1.3    Typical Use Cases for Ajax

In addition to the example described in the previous section of the search process running in the background, there are a number of other examples of using Ajax, which we’ll briefly present ahead.

#### Automatic Completion of Input Fields

A classic example is the completion of input fields. The idea is to display input suggestions to the user in the form of a selection list while the user enters text in the corresponding input field (see [Figure 9.6](#09_001.html_f9.6)), thus preselecting possible selection values. Technically, you register an event listener for the <samp class="listingcharacter">change</samp> event of the respective input field, use Ajax to send a request containing the current input to the server, and display the matching values returned by the server in the dropdown list.

[![Automatic Completion of Input Fields](bilderklein/klein09_006.png)](img-f9.6.html)

**Figure 9.6** Automatic Completion of Input Fields

#### Pagination of Large Records

Another example is the pagination of records (i.e., splitting them into individual pages). Indeed, if there are many different records (e.g., a table of users), it makes sense not to display all records in one long table, but only a part of the data at a time, with the option to switch back and forth between individual parts. As a rule, a navigation option is provided above or below the corresponding table, as shown in [Figure 9.7](#09_001.html_f9.7).

[![Ajax Is Often Used for Pagination](bilderklein/klein09_007.png)](img-f9.7.html)

**Figure 9.7**     Ajax Is Often Used for Pagination

The example can be implemented by first loading only a part of the records from the server via Ajax (the “first page,” so to speak, similar to the search results described earlier). If the user now clicks on the link to another page, the records for this selected page are loaded from the server accordingly.

#### News Tickers

News tickers, which you may see on news or sports pages, use Ajax to make regular requests to the server and display new messages, if available. To do this, you use the <samp class="listingcharacter">setInterval()</samp> method on the client side (see [Chapter 8](#08_001.html_h8)) to send requests to the server at specific intervals via Ajax. If the requests return new messages, these are incorporated into the news ticker accordingly.

#### Editable UI Components

The concept of Ajax has greatly propelled the proliferation of web applications—that is, web pages that look and feel like classic desktop applications while running in the browser. Tables that allow you to edit individual records are one of the many GUI components used in such applications (see [Figure 9.8](#09_001.html_f9.8)). Usually, you can start the edit mode by double-clicking on a table cell and then adjust the value in the cell. In the background, the corresponding record is then synchronized with the database on the server via Ajax.

[![Simple Editing of Table Records via Ajax](bilderklein/klein09_008.png)](img-f9.8.html)

**Figure 9.8**     Simple Editing of Table Records via Ajax

###### Note

Beyond these use cases, there are plenty of others where Ajax comes in handy. In general, Ajax is useful whenever you want to dynamically load data from or send data to the server without reloading the web page.

### 9.1.4    Data Formats Used

Now the question arises, what data is transferred between client and server, and in what format? In principle, you can use any format, but the following three are used most frequently:

*   HTML
    This format is useful if you want to load ready-made GUI components (also called widgets; e.g., calendar components or the like) directly from the server and integrate them into the web page. We'll show you how to use HTML as a data format in [Section 9.4.2](#09_004.html_h9.4.2).

*   Extensible Markup Language (XML)
    This format is suitable if you load structured data from the server (e.g., individual records for a table) and want to generate content on the web page based on this data. We'll show you how to use XML as a data format in [Section 9.4.3](#09_004.html_h9.4.3). But first, we'll give you an introduction to this format in [Section 9.2](#09_002.html_h9.2).

*   JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)
    Like XML, this format is suitable whenever you want to load data from the server to generate content on the web page based on that data, but it’s much leaner than XML and comparatively easy to process in JavaScript applications. We'll show you how to use JSON as a data format in [Section 9.4.4](#09_004.html_h9.4.4). The structure of this format is explained in [Section 9.3](#09_003.html_h9.3).

###### Various Exchange Formats

Obviously, the term Asynchronous JavaScript and XML is actually misleading because not only XML can be used as an exchange format.

## 9.2    The XML Format

XML is a markup language that can be used to structure data hierarchically.

### 9.2.1    The Structure of XML

In terms of syntax, XML looks similar to HTML (although there are some differences in detail, which we won't discuss at this point); that is, there are XML elements and XML attributes.

In principle, you’re free to decide which elements you use within an XML document and which attributes you use within an element. As a rule, however, both are defined in an XML schema (or alternatively in a document type definition [DTD]). Both the XML schema and DTD contain rules, including which elements may be used in an XML document, which attributes these elements may have, and which child elements are allowed. As this book is primarily about JavaScript and not about XML, we’ll stick to this general information regarding XML schema and DTD.

As an example, take a look at [Listing 9.1](#09_002.html_l9.1), which shows a typical XML document. The first line contains information about the XML version used and the encoding; the rest of the document represents the actual content. The <samp class="listingcharacter"><artists></samp> element represents the root node in this example. As with HTML, there can only be one of these within a document.

Below <samp class="listingcharacter"><artists></samp>, there are two child elements of the type <samp class="listingcharacter"><artist></samp>, each of which has a <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> attribute and also a child element of the type <samp class="listingcharacter"><albums></samp>. The latter, in turn, has several child elements of the type <samp class="listingcharacter"><album></samp>, each of which contains two child elements, <samp class="listingcharacter"><title></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter"><year></samp>.

```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<artists>
  <artist name="Kyuss">
    <albums>
      <album>
        <title>Wretch</title>
        <year>1991</year>
      </album>
      <album>
        <title>Blues for the Red Sun</title>
        <year>1992</year>
      </album>
      <album>
        <title>Welcome to Sky Valley</title>
        <year>1994</year>
      </album>
      <album>
        <title>...And the Circus Leaves Town</title>
        <year>1995</year>
      </album>
    </albums>
  </artist>
  <artist name="Ben Harper">
    <albums>
      <album>
        <title>The Will to Live</title>
        <year>1997</year>
      </album>
      <album>
        <title>Burn to Shine</title>
        <year>1999</year>
      </album>
      <album>
        <title>Live from Mars</title>
        <year>2001</year>
      </album>
      <album>
        <title>Diamonds on the Inside</title>
        <year>2003</year>
      </album>
    </albums>
  </artist>
</artists> 
```

**Listing 9.1**     Example of an XML File

###### Note

XML files typically have the .xml file extension.

### 9.2.2    XML and the DOM API

Because of their hierarchical structure, it makes sense to represent XML documents as a tree. For example, [Figure 9.9](#09_002.html_f9.9) shows the XML tree for the example in [Listing 9.1](#09_002.html_l9.1).

[![Hierarchical Tree Representation of an XML Document](bilderklein/klein09_009.png)](img-f9.9.html)

**Figure 9.9**     Hierarchical Tree Representation of an XML Document

Of course, you will have noticed immediately that the XML tree bears a strong resemblance to the DOM tree (see [Chapter 5](#05_001.html_h5)). This is no coincidence: the DOM API is also used for XML documents, so the contents of XML documents can be accessed in the same way as we discussed for HTML documents in [Chapter 5](#05_001.html_h5). We’ll show you examples later in this chapter in [Section 9.2](#09_002.html_h9.2) and [Section 9.4.3](#09_004.html_h9.4.3)).

###### Note

More precisely, XML data within a JavaScript program is represented by the type <samp class="listingcharacter">Document</samp> in the same way as for web pages (i.e., the object stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter">document</samp> variable).

### 9.2.3    Converting Strings to XML Objects

When you send XML data to a server via Ajax or, conversely, retrieve XML data from a server via Ajax, the data is converted in the background. When XML objects (of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Document</samp> type) are converted into strings, this is called data serialization. The process of converting strings into XML objects, on the other hand, is called parsing. In principle, you don't need to know how both work, but having a bit of background knowledge in this regard certainly doesn't hurt.

To create XML objects based on a string that contains data in XML format, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">DOMParser</samp> object. Its <samp class="listingcharacter">parseFormString()</samp> method can be passed the corresponding string as the first argument and the MIME type (usually <samp class="listingcharacter">text/xml</samp>) as the second argument. Provided that the passed string contains valid XML, you get an object of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Document</samp> type that contains the parsed XML (see also [Figure 9.10](#09_002.html_f9.10)). [Listing 9.2](#09_002.html_l9.2) shows a corresponding example. You see that the DOM selection methods you’re already familiar with, like <samp class="listingcharacter">querySelector()</samp>, can be called on the parsed XML object to select individual elements in the XML tree.

[![The DOMParser Object Can Be Used to Convert Strings into XML Objects](bilderklein/klein09_010.png)](img-f9.10.html)

**Figure 9.10**     The DOMParser Object Can Be Used to Convert Strings into XML Objects

```
const xmlString = `<?xml version="1.0" encoding="ISO-8859-1"?>
                <artists>
                  <artist name="Kyuss">
                    <albums>
                      <album>
                        <title>Wretch</title>
                        <year>1991</year>
                      </album>
                    </albums>
                  </artist>
                </artists>`;
const domParser = new DOMParser();
const xmlDOM = domParser.parseFromString(xmlString, 'text/xml');
const firstArtist = xmlDOM.querySelector('artist');
console.log(firstArtist.getAttribute('name'));                  // "Kyuss"
console.log(firstArtist.querySelector('title').textContent);    // "Wretch"
console.log(firstArtist.querySelector('year').textContent);     // 1991
