You can find some examples of using these selectors in [Listing 10.10](#10_002.html_l10.10), and complete lists of all corresponding selectors can be found in the tables ahead.

```
$(document).ready(() => {
  const inputElements = $('input');          // all <input> elements
  const john = $('#john');                   // element with the ID "john"
  const oddElements = $('.odd');             // elements of the class "odd"
  const elements = $('td, th');              // all <td>- und <th> elements
  const inputJohn = $('input[name="john"]'); // <input> elements the
                                             // name attribute of which  
                                             // has the value "john"
  const oddRows = $('tr').odd());            // all "odd" <tr> elements
  const evenRows = $('tr').even();           // all "even" <tr> elements
  const listItemsAtIndex = $('li:eq(2)');    // all <li> elements at index 2
  const allOthers = $(':not(li)');           // all elements other than <li>
  const notExample = $(':not(.example)');    // all elements without the CSS 
                                             // class "example"
}); 
```

**Listing 10.10**     A Few Examples of Using Selectors

###### Note

Some selectors such as <samp class="listingcharacter">:odd</samp> (for selecting all "odd" elements), <samp class="listingcharacter">:even</samp> (for selecting all "even" elements), <samp class="listingcharacter">:first</samp> (for selecting the first elements), and <samp class="listingcharacter">:last</samp> (for selecting the last elements) are deprecated since jQuery 3.4\. Instead, you should first select the elements using the appropriate selector and apply the <samp class="listingcharacter">odd()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">even()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">first()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">last()</samp> methods on the result set (see [Listing 10.10](#10_002.html_l10.10) for the use of <samp class="listingcharacter">odd()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">even()</samp>).

###### Combination of Selectors

The individual selectors naturally can be combined with each other, as you know from CSS.

### 10.2.2    Accessing and Modifying Content

After you’ve selected elements via the jQuery method using the selectors presented in the previous section, the jQuery object provides various methods for the selected elements to access and modify the content. These include but are not limited to the following:

*   Accessing and modifying HTML and text content (see [Table 10.9](#10_002.html_t10.9))

*   Adding content within an element (see [Table 10.10](#10_002.html_t10.10) and [Figure 10.1](#10_002.html_f10.1))

*   Adding content outside an element (see [Table 10.11](#10_002.html_t10.11) and [Figure 10.1](#10_002.html_f10.1))

*   Adding content around an element (see [Table 10.12](#10_002.html_t10.12))

*   Replacing content (see [Table 10.13](#10_002.html_t10.13))

*   Removing content (see [Table 10.14](#10_002.html_t10.14))

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">html()</samp> | Without an argument, this method returns the HTML content of an element. With an argument, this method sets the HTML content of an element. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">text()</samp> | Without an argument, this method returns the text content of an element. With an argument, this method sets the text content of an element. |

**Table 10.9**     Methods for Retrieving and Defining Content

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">append()</samp> | Adds content to the end of the selected elements: <samp class="listingcharacter">$(a).append(b)</samp> adds content <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> to the end of element <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> (see [Figure 10.1](#10_002.html_f10.1)). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">appendTo()</samp> | Opposite of <samp class="listingcharacter">append()</samp>; that is, <samp class="listingcharacter">$(a).appendTo(b)</samp> adds element <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> as content to the end of element <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">prepend()</samp> | Inserts content at the beginning of the selected elements: <samp class="listingcharacter">$(a).prepend(b)</samp> adds content <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> to the beginning of element <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> (see [Figure 10.1](#10_002.html_f10.1)). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">prependTo()</samp> | Opposite of <samp class="listingcharacter">prepend()</samp>; that is, <samp class="listingcharacter">$(a).prependTo(b)</samp> adds element <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> as content to the beginning of element <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp>. |

**Table 10.10**     Methods for Adding Content within an Element

[![The Different Methods for Adding Content inside and outside Elements](bilderklein/klein10_001.png)](img-f10.1.html)

**Figure 10.1** The Different Methods for Adding Content inside and outside Elements

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">after()</samp> | Adds content after each of the selected elements: <samp class="listingcharacter">$(a).after(b)</samp> inserts content <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> after element <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> (see [Figure 10.1](#10_002.html_f10.1)). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">before()</samp> | Adds content before each of the selected elements: <samp class="listingcharacter">$(a).before(b)</samp> inserts content <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> before element <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> (see [Figure 10.1](#10_002.html_f10.1)). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">insertAfter()</samp> | Opposite of <samp class="listingcharacter">after()</samp>; that is, <samp class="listingcharacter">$(a).insertAfter(b)</samp> inserts element <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> after element <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">insertBefore()</samp> | Opposite of <samp class="listingcharacter">before()</samp>; that is, <samp class="listingcharacter">$(a).insertBefore(b)</samp> inserts element <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> before element <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp>. |

**Table 10.11**     Methods for Adding Content outside an Element

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> | Creates a copy of the selected elements. More precisely, a so-called deep copy is created, which also copies child elements of the selected elements. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">wrap()</samp> | Adds new content around each of the selected elements. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">wrapAll()</samp> | Adds new content around all selected elements. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">wrapInner()</samp> | Adds new content around the content of each of the selected elements. |

**Table 10.12**     Methods for Adding Content around an Element

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">replaceWith()</samp> | Replaces the selected elements with new content: <samp class="listingcharacter">$(a).replaceWith(b)</samp> replaces element <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> with content <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">replaceAll()</samp> | Opposite of <samp class="listingcharacter">replaceWith()</samp>; that is, <samp class="listingcharacter">$(a).replaceAll(b)</samp> replaces all elements selected by selector <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> with the content in <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp>. |

**Table 10.13**     Methods for Replacing Content

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">detach()</samp> | Removes the selected elements from the DOM tree but retains references to the removed elements so that they can be reincorporated into the DOM tree at a later time |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">empty()</samp> | Removes all child nodes from the selected elements |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">remove()</samp> | Removes the selected elements from the DOM tree |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">unwrap()</samp> | Removes the parent element from each of the selected elements |

**Table 10.14**     Methods for Removing Content

Some examples of these methods are shown in [Listing 10.11](#10_002.html_l10.11). For example, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">html()</samp> method to access the HTML content, the <samp class="listingcharacter">text()</samp> method to access the text content (both read and write access), <samp class="listingcharacter">append()</samp> to append new content to the existing content of the selected elements, <samp class="listingcharacter">prepend()</samp> to insert content before the existing content, <samp class="listingcharacter">after()</samp> to append new content to the selected elements, and <samp class="listingcharacter">before()</samp> to insert content before the selected elements.

```
// Add new HTML content
$('#main').html('<div>New content</div>');
// Access the HTML content
const htmlContent = $('#main').html();

// Add new text content
$('#main').text('New text content');
// Access the text content
const textContent = $('#main').text();

// Add new content after the 
// existing content of each <div> element
// with the CSS class "example"
$('div.example').append('<p>Example</p>');

// Add new content before the 
// existing content of each <div> element
// with the CSS class "example"
$('div.example').prepend('<p>Example</p>');

// Add new content after each 
// <div> element with the CSS class "example"
$('div.example').after('<p>Example</p>');

// Add new content before each 
// <div> element with the CSS class "example"
$('div.example').before('<p>Example</p>'); 
```

**Listing 10.11**     Some Examples of Changing and Adding Content

### 10.2.3    Filtering Selected Elements

The jQuery object also provides various methods for the selected elements, which you can use to further narrow down the currently selected elements (see [Table 10.15](#10_002.html_t10.15)). Some examples are shown in [Listing 10.12](#10_002.html_l10.12): for example, the <samp class="listingcharacter">eq()</samp> method limits the selection to the element at index 2 (i.e., the third <samp class="listingcharacter"><li></samp> element in the example); the <samp class="listingcharacter">first()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">last()</samp> methods let you select the first and last of the currently selected elements, respectively; the <samp class="listingcharacter">filter()</samp> method limits the selection to the specified selector; and the <samp class="listingcharacter">not()</samp> method limits the selection to the elements that do not match the specified selector. You can also use the <samp class="listingcharacter">has()</samp> method to select the elements that have at least one child element that matches the given selector. [Figure 10.2](#10_002.html_f10.2) illustrates the filter methods shown in [Listing 10.12](#10_002.html_l10.12).

```
// Selection of the third <li> element
$('li').eq(2);
// Selection of the first <li> element
$('li').first();
// Selection of <li> elements that have the CSS class ".selected"
$('li').filter('.selected');
// Selection of all <li> elements that contain a <ul> element
$('li').has('ul');
// Selection of all elements that have the CSS class ".selected"
$('li').has('.selected');
// Selection of the last <li> element
$('li').last();
// Selection of all class attributes of the <li> elements
$('li').map(() => { this.className });
// Selection of all <li> elements that do not have the CSS class ".selected"
$('li').not('.selected');
// Selection of the first two <li> elements
$('li').slice(0, 2); 
```

**Listing 10.12**     Usage of Different Filter Methods

[![Narrowing Down Elements via jQuery Filter Methods](bilderklein/klein10_002.png)](img-f10.2.html)

**Figure 10.2** Narrowing Down Elements via jQuery Filter Methods

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">add()</samp> | Adds new elements to a selection of elements |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">addBack()</samp> | Adds a previous selection to the current selection of elements |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">eq()</samp> | Reduces the selected elements to one element at a given index |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">filter()</samp> | Reduces the selected elements to those elements (1) that match the passed selector or (2) for which the passed filter function returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">find()</samp> | Selects the child elements of the selected elements that (1) match the passed selector, (2) are contained in the passed jQuery object, or (3) are equal to the passed element |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">first()</samp> | Reduces the selected elements to the first element |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">has()</samp> | Reduces the selected elements to those elements that have a child element that (1) matches the passed selector or (2) is equal to the passed element |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">is()</samp> | Checks if at least one of the selected elements (1) matches the passed selector, (2) returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> for the passed filter function, (3) is contained in the passed jQuery object, or (4) is one of the elements passed as parameter |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">last()</samp> | Reduces the selected elements to the last element |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">not()</samp> | Reduces the selected elements to those that (1) do not match the passed selector, (2) do not match the passed filter function, or (3) are not contained in the passed jQuery object |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">slice()</samp> | Reduces the selected elements to a subset defined by start and end index |

**Table 10.15**     Methods for Filtering

### 10.2.4    Accessing Attributes

The jQuery object also provides some methods to access HTML attributes (see [Table 10.16](#10_002.html_t10.16)). The <samp class="listingcharacter">attr()</samp> method can be used to determine or reset values of attributes, as shown in [Listing 10.13](#10_002.html_l10.13): if you pass the name of an attribute to the method, the method returns the corresponding value of the attribute; if, on the other hand, you pass another string as the second argument to the method, this string is used as the new value for the attribute.

Alternatively, you can pass an object to the method in order to add several attributes in one go. In this case, the object's property names are used as names for the attributes, and the object property values are used as values for the attributes.

To delete attributes, however, use the <samp class="listingcharacter">removeAttr()</samp> method. For adding and removing CSS classes, the methods <samp class="listingcharacter">addClass()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">removeClass()</samp> are available. However, these two methods are actually redundant—at least for newer browsers that support the <samp class="listingcharacter">classList</samp> property, which provide equivalent functionality via the <samp class="listingcharacter">add()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">remove()</samp> methods.

```
const element = $('a#main');
// Read access to the "href" attribute of the element
const href = element.attr('href');
// Write access to the "href" attribute of the element
element.attr('href', 'index.html');
// Alternative write access via configuration object
element.attr({
  href: 'index.html',
  target: '_blank'
});
// Remove the "href" attribute from the element
element.removeAttr('href');
// Add a CSS class
element.addClass('highlighted');
// Remove a CSS class
element.removeClass('highlighted'); 
```

**Listing 10.13**     Access to Attributes and CSS Classes

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">attr()</samp> | With one argument, this method returns the value for an attribute (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">$(’a#main’).attr(’href’)</samp>). With two arguments, this method sets the value of an attribute (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">$('a#main').attr('href', 'index.html')</samp>). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">removeAttr()</samp> | Removes an attribute from an element, e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">$('a#main').removeAttr ('href')</samp>). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">addClass()</samp> | Adds a new CSS class to the values in the <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> attribute. In newer browsers, this is possible without jQuery thanks to the standardized <samp class="listingcharacter">classList</samp> property and its <samp class="listingcharacter">add()</samp> method. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">removeClass()</samp> | Removes a CSS class from the values in the <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> attribute. This too is possible in newer browsers without jQuery thanks to the <samp class="listingcharacter">classList</samp> property and its <samp class="listingcharacter">remove()</samp> method. However, the <samp class="listingcharacter">removeClass()</samp> method can alternatively be passed a function that returns a comma-separated list of CSS classes. This functionality isn’t possible via the <samp class="listingcharacter">remove()</samp> method of the <samp class="listingcharacter">classList</samp> property. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">toggleClass()</samp> | Toggles a CSS class: if the element has the passed class, the class will be removed, and if the element doesn’t have the passed class, the class will be added. |

**Table 10.16**     Methods for Accessing Attributes and CSS Classes

### 10.2.5    Accessing CSS Properties

To access CSS properties, jQuery provides the <samp class="listingcharacter">css()</samp> method. Like other methods, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">html()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">text()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">attr()</samp>, this method can be used to both read and set values. For the former, pass the method the name of the CSS property of which the value is to be read; for the latter, specify the value to be set as the second parameter.

Alternatively, as with the <samp class="listingcharacter">attr()</samp> method, an object can be passed as an argument, and the respective properties are then used as CSS properties. In addition, you can also pass an array of strings as an argument to read the values of several CSS properties in one step. Some examples are shown in [Listing 10.14](#10_002.html_l10.14).

```
// Read the background color of the <body> element
const backgroundColor = $('body').css('background-color');
// Read the foreground color and the background color of the <body> element
const properties = $('body').css(['color', 'background-color']);
// Set the background color of the <body> element
$('body').css('background-color', 'blue');
// Set the foreground color and the background color of the <body> element
$('body').css({
 'color': 'white', 
 'background-color': 'blue'
}); 
```

**Listing 10.14**     Accessing CSS Properties

### 10.2.6    Navigating between Elements

Starting from a selection of elements stored in a jQuery object, you can use the methods presented ahead to find elements that have a specific relationship to these elements, such as parent elements, sibling elements, and child elements. Some examples are shown in [Listing 10.15](#10_002.html_l10.15). The corresponding descriptions of the methods can be found in [Table 10.17](#10_002.html_t10.17).

```
// Child elements
// Selection of all child elements of <ul>
const listItems = $('ul').children();
// Selection of the next link within <ul>
const closestLink = $('ul').closest('a');

// Sibling elements
// Selection of the next sibling element
const nextSibling = $('ul').next();
// Selection of the next link element
const nextSiblingLink = $('ul').next('a');
// Selection of all next sibling elements
const nextSiblings = $('ul').nextAll();
// Selection of all next link elements
const nextSiblingLinks = $('div').nextAll('a');
// Selection of all next sibling elements up to the specified element
const nextSiblingsUntil = $('div').nextUntil('a');
// Selection of the previous sibling element
const previousSibling = $('ul').prev();
// Selection of all previous sibling elements
const previousSiblings = $('ul').prevAll();
// Selection of all previous sibling elements up to the specified element
const previousSiblingsUntil = $('div').prevUntil('a');
// Selection of all sibling elements
const siblings = $('div').siblings();

// Parent elements
// Selection of the parent element
const parent = $('ul').parent();
// Selection of all parent elements
const parents = $('ul').parents();
// Selection of all parent elements up to the specified element
const parentsUntil = $('ul').parentsUntil('div'); 
```

**Listing 10.15**     Various Examples of Navigating between Elements

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">children()</samp> | Selects the child elements of the selected elements. Optionally, a selector can be passed--in that case only those child elements are selected to which this selector applies.. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">closest()</samp> | Selects the first element of the selected elements that matches the selector passed as a parameter or for which one of the parent elements matches the selector. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">next()</samp> | Selects the next sibling element of the selected elements. If a selector is passed, the next sibling element that matches this selector is selected. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">nextAll()</samp> | Selects all next sibling elements of the selected elements. If a selector is passed, the next sibling elements that match this selector are selected. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">nextUntil()</samp> | Selects all next sibling elements of the selected elements. If a selector is passed, the next sibling elements are selected up to the sibling element that matches this selector. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">parent()</samp> | Selects the parent element of the selected elements. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">parents()</samp> | Selects all parent elements preceding in the hierarchy of the selected elements. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">parentsUntil()</samp> | Selects all parent elements preceding in the hierarchy of the selected elements up to an element that (1) matches the passed selector, (2) matches the passed element, or (3) is contained in the passed jQuery object. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">prev()</samp> | Selects the previous sibling element of the selected elements. If a selector is passed, the previous sibling element that matches this selector is selected. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">prevAll()</samp> | Selects all previous sibling elements of the selected elements. If a selector is passed, the previous sibling elements that match this selector are selected. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">prevUntil()</samp> | Selects all previous sibling elements of the selected elements. If a selector is passed, the previous sibling elements are selected up to the sibling element that matches this selector. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">siblings()</samp> | Selects all sibling elements of the selected elements. If a selector is passed, the sibling elements that match this selector are selected. |

**Table 10.17**     Methods for Navigating the DOM Tree

### 10.2.7    Using Effects and Animations

Effects such as fading in or out elements of a web page were not always as easy to implement as they are now with the help of CSS3 animations. It’s little wonder then that jQuery offers several methods for this as well, the most important of which are shown in [Table 10.18](#10_002.html_t10.18). For example, with <samp class="listingcharacter">fadeIn()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">fadeOut()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">fadeToggle()</samp>, it’s possible to fade the selected elements in and out, and <samp class="listingcharacter">slideDown()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">slideUp()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">slideToggle()</samp> enable you to slide the selected elements in and out.

The most flexible option is provided by <samp class="listingcharacter">animate()</samp>. This method can be passed—in the form of a configuration object—various CSS properties to be animated, the speed or duration of the animation (either as a string, such as one of the values <samp class="listingcharacter">fast</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">slow</samp>, or as a numeric value specifying the duration in milliseconds), an easing function (which describes how the speed of the animation behaves in relation to the time within the animation), and a callback function that’s called when the animation has been fully executed (see [Listing 10.16](#10_002.html_l10.16)).

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">animate()</samp> | Enables the animation of CSS properties. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">clearQueue()</samp> | Removes all animations from the queue that have not yet been executed. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">delay()</samp> | Delays an animation by a specified number of milliseconds. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">dequeue()</samp> | Executes the next animation in the queue. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">fadeIn()</samp> | Fades the selected elements in. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">fadeOut()</samp> | Fades the selected elements out. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">fadeTo()</samp> | Adjusts the opacity of the selected elements. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">fadeToggle()</samp> | Fades the selected elements in or out, depending on their state: if an element is visible, it’s faded out, but if it isn’t visible, it’s faded in. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">finish()</samp> | Stops the current animation, removes all animations from the queue, and sets the CSS properties of the selected elements to the target value. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">hide()</samp> | Hides the selected elements. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">queue()</samp> | Accesses the animations in the queue. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">show()</samp> | Shows the selected elements. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">slideDown()</samp> | Slides the selected elements down, from top to bottom. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">slideToggle()</samp> | Slides the selected elements in or out, depending on their state: if an element is visible, it slides out from bottom to the, but if it isn’t visible, it slides in from top to bottom. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">slideUp()</samp> | Slides the selected elements up, from bottom to top. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">stop()</samp> | Stops the current animation. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">toggle()</samp> | Hides or displays the selected elements: if an element is visible, it’s hidden, but if it isn’t visible, it’s displayed. |

**Table 10.18**     Methods for Displaying and Hiding Elements

```
'use strict';
$(document).ready(() => {
  $('main').animate(
    { opacity: 0.75 }, // Properties
    'fast',            // Speed
    'swing',           // Easing 
    () => {
      // Animation completed
    }
  );
}); 
```

## 10.3    Responding to Events

As you recall from [Chapter 6](#06_001.html_h6), there are several options for catching events. Event handlers are usually available for the corresponding event, and there’s also the possibility to register several event listeners for one event via the <samp class="listingcharacter">addEventListener()</samp> method. Older versions of Internet Explorer also use the <samp class="listingcharacter">attachEvent()</samp> method, which fulfills a similar task.

We also showed a corresponding browser-independent helper function in [Chapter 6](#06_001.html_h6). The jQuery library offers a browser-independent solution as well.

### 10.3.1    Registering Event Listeners

jQuery provides several methods to respond to events or register event listeners. So, on the one hand, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">on()</samp> method, which is called on the jQuery object, as shown in [Listing 10.17](#10_003.html_l10.17): you pass the name of the event to be responded to as the first parameter and the event listener in the form of a function as the second parameter.

```
$('#button').on('click', (event) => {
  console.log('Button pressed');
}); 
```

**Listing 10.17**     Registering an Event Listener

###### Note

If the jQuery object contains references to multiple elements, calling an event method for each element in the selection invokes the corresponding event listener.

As an alternative to the general <samp class="listingcharacter">on()</samp> method, jQuery offers various methods named specifically after the event to be caught, such as the <samp class="listingcharacter">click()</samp> method found in [Listing 10.18](#10_003.html_l10.18). Logically, these event methods don’t need to be passed the name of the respective event as a parameter, but only the event listener.

```
$('#button').click((event) => {
  console.log('Button pressed');
}); 
```

**Listing 10.18**     Registering an Event Listener via the Shorthand Method

Overall, the event methods can be classified as follows:

*   General event methods (see [Table 10.19](#10_003.html_t10.19))

*   Event methods for handling general events ([Section 10.3.2](#10_003.html_h10.3.2))

*   Event methods for handling mouse events ([Section 10.3.3](#10_003.html_h10.3.3))

*   Event methods for handling keyboard events ([Section 10.3.4](#10_003.html_h10.3.4))

*   Event methods for handling form events ([Section 10.3.5](#10_003.html_h10.3.5))

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">bind()</samp> | Adds an event listener for an event. Since jQuery 1.7, however, the <samp class="listingcharacter">on()</samp> method should be used according to the official documentation. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">delegate()</samp> | For older jQuery versions, this is the preferred method to add an event listener for an event. However, since jQuery 1.7, the <samp class="listingcharacter">on()</samp> method should be used. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">off()</samp> | Removes an event listener for an event. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">on()</samp> | Adds an event listener for an event. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">one()</samp> | Adds an event listener that is triggered at most once per event for each selected element. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">trigger()</samp> | Runs all event listeners registered for an event. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">triggerHandler()</samp> | Like the <samp class="listingcharacter">trigger()</samp> method, but doesn’t perform the default behavior for an event (such as submitting a form). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">unbind()</samp> | Removes an event listener for an event. Since jQuery 1.7, however, the <samp class="listingcharacter">off()</samp> method should be used according to the official documentation. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">undelegate()</samp> | For older jQuery versions, this is the preferred method to remove an event listener for an event. However, since jQuery 1.7, the <samp class="listingcharacter">off()</samp> method should be used. |

**Table 10.19**     Methods for Managing Event Handlers

### 10.3.2    Responding to General Events

[Table 10.20](#10_003.html_t10.20) contains some methods for registering event listeners for general events: <samp class="listingcharacter">error()</samp> enables you to register event listeners that are triggered when an <samp class="listingcharacter">error</samp> event is raised on the selected elements, event listeners registered via <samp class="listingcharacter">ready()</samp> are called as soon as the corresponding elements have been loaded (see [Listing 10.19](#10_003.html_l10.19)), event listeners registered via <samp class="listingcharacter">resize()</samp> are called whenever a <samp class="listingcharacter">resize</samp> event occurs for the elements, and event listeners registered via <samp class="listingcharacter">scroll()</samp> are called whenever a <samp class="listingcharacter">scroll</samp> event occurs for the elements.

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">error()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when an <samp class="listingcharacter">error</samp> event occurs. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ready()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when the DOM or the element passed to the method is fully loaded. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">resize()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when a <samp class="listingcharacter">resize</samp> event occurs. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">scroll()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when an element is scrolled. |

**Table 10.20**     Different Methods for Registering Event Listeners

```
$(document).ready(() => {
  console.log('Web page loaded');
}); 
```

**Listing 10.19**     Registering an Event Listener for Loading the Document

### 10.3.3    Responding to Mouse Events

[Table 10.21](#10_003.html_t10.21) shows the methods jQuery uses to register event listeners for mouse events. They basically correspond to the events you already know from [Chapter 6](#06_001.html_h6): <samp class="listingcharacter">click()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">dbclick()</samp> for mouse clicks; <samp class="listingcharacter">focusin()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">focusout()</samp> for focusing elements; and <samp class="listingcharacter">mousedown()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">mouseenter()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">mouseleave()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">mousemove()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">mouseout()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">mouseover()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">mouseup()</samp> for mouse movements over elements.

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">click()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when the mouse is clicked |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">dblclick()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when the mouse is double-clicked |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">focusin()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when an element receives focus |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">focusout()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when an element loses focus |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">hover()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when the mouse pointer hovers over an element |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">mousedown()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when the mouse pointer is over an element and the mouse button is pressed |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">mouseenter()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when the mouse pointer enters an element |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">mouseleave()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when the mouse pointer leaves an element |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">mousemove()</samp> | Register event listeners that are triggered when the mouse moves over an element |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">mouseout()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when the mouse pointer leaves an element |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">mouseover()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when the mouse pointer enters an element |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">mouseup()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when the mouse pointer is over an element and the mouse button is released |

**Table 10.21**     Methods for Handling Mouse Events

An example is shown in [Listing 10.20](#10_003.html_l10.20).

```
$('button#target').click((event) => {
  console.log('Button was pressed');
}); 
```

**Listing 10.20**     Registering an Event Listener for a Mouse Event

By the way, it’s also possible to use the event methods not for registering event listeners, but for triggering events. To do this, simply call the corresponding method without any arguments. In [Listing 10.21](#10_003.html_l10.21), for example, within the second event listener (registered on the <samp class="listingcharacter"><button></samp> element with the ID <samp class="listingcharacter">target2</samp>), the <samp class="listingcharacter">click</samp> event is triggered for the <samp class="listingcharacter"><button></samp> element with the ID <samp class="listingcharacter">target</samp>.

```
$('button#target').click((event) => {
  console.log('Button was pressed');
});
$('button#target2').click((event) => {
  $('button#target').click();
}); 
```

**Listing 10.21**     Triggering an Event

###### Note

Most methods in jQuery can be called with a different number of arguments, and each has different functions. For example, as shown earlier in this chapter, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">attr()</samp> method to both read and write HTML attributes or, as just shown, you can use the event methods to both register event listeners and trigger events.

### 10.3.4    Responding to Keyboard Events

For registering event listeners for keyboard events, the methods listed in [Table 10.22](#10_003.html_t10.22) are available: <samp class="listingcharacter">keydown()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">keyup()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">keypress()</samp> for registering event listeners that are triggered when a key is pressed or released. Again, all of this should be familiar from [Chapter 6](#06_001.html_h6).

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">keydown()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when a key on the keyboard is pressed. If a key is pressed for a longer time, the event listener is executed several times. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">keypress()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when a key on the keyboard is pressed. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">keyup()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when a key on the keyboard is released. |

**Table 10.22**     Methods for Handling Keyboard Events

An example of using these methods is shown in [Listing 10.22](#10_003.html_l10.22). This nicely illustrates how the individual event methods (or all jQuery methods in general) can be used one after the other.

```
$('input#username')
  .keypress((event) => {
    console.log('Key for entering username pressed.');
  })
  .keydown((event) => {
    console.log('Key is pressed.');
  })
  .keyup((event) => {
    console.log('Key for entering username released.');
  }); 
```

**Listing 10.22**     Registering Different Event Listeners for Keyboard Events

###### Fluent API

When an API allows you to call a method directly on the return value of a method, as in [Listing 10.22](#10_003.html_l10.22), it is also called a fluent API.

### 10.3.5    Responding to Form Events

The methods listed in [Table 10.23](#10_003.html_t10.23) for registering event listeners related to form events should also be essentially familiar from [Chapter 6](#06_001.html_h6): <samp class="listingcharacter">blur()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">focus()</samp> for registering event listeners that are triggered when a form field loses or receives focus, <samp class="listingcharacter">change()</samp> when the value of a form field changes, <samp class="listingcharacter">select()</samp> when a specific value is selected for a form field, and <samp class="listingcharacter">submit()</samp> when a form is submitted.

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">blur()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when a form field loses focus |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">change()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when the selected value of a selection list, a checkbox, or a group of radio buttons has been changed |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">focus()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when a form field receives focus |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">select()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when the text of an input field (<samp class="listingcharacter"><input></samp> element of the <samp class="listingcharacter">text</samp> type) or a text input area (<samp class="listingcharacter"><textarea></samp> element) is selected |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">submit()</samp> | Register event listeners that are executed when a form is submitted |

**Table 10.23**     Methods for Handling Form Events

Some examples are shown in [Listing 10.23](#10_003.html_l10.23).

```
$('input#username')
  .focus((event) => {
    console.log('Input field focused.');
  })
  .blur((event) => {
    console.log('Input field no longer focused.');
  })
  .change((event) => {
    console.log('Text changed.');
  })
  .select((event) => {
    console.log('Text selected.');
  }); 
```

**Listing 10.23**     Registering Different Event Listeners for Form Events

### 10.3.6    Accessing Information from Events

The event object, which is available as a parameter within each event listener, contains different information and provides different methods, as shown in [Table 10.24](#10_003.html_t10.24). Basically, this is the information also contained in the standard event object, as discussed in [Chapter 6](#06_001.html_h6), supplemented by a few more details. But again, jQuery hides the browser-specific details, allowing for browser-independent use.

| Property/Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">currentTarget</samp> | Contains the current element during the bubbling phase |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">data</samp> | Contains an optional data object passed to the event method |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">delegateTarget</samp> | Contains the element on which the event listener was registered |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">isDefaultPrevented()</samp> | Indicates whether <samp class="listingcharacter">preventDefault()</samp> was called on the event object |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">isImmediatePropagationStopped()</samp> | Indicates whether <samp class="listingcharacter">stopImmediatePropagation()</samp> was called on the event object |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">isPropagationStopped()</samp> | Indicates whether <samp class="listingcharacter">stopPropagation()</samp> was called on the event object |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">metaKey</samp> | Contains an indication of whether the so-called meta key (for Mac keyboards, the (cmd) key; for Windows keyboards, the (Windows) key) was pressed while the event was triggered. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace</samp> | Contains the namespace of the event |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">pageX</samp> | Contains the mouse position relative to the left edge of the document |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">pageY</samp> | Contains the mouse position relative to the top of the document |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">preventDefault()</samp> | Prevents the default action for an event from being executed |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">relatedTarget</samp> | For an element for which an event was triggered, contains the element directly related to the event (e.g., in the case of a <samp class="listingcharacter">mouseout</samp> event, the element on which the <samp class="listingcharacter">mouseover</samp> event was triggered by the same user action) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">result</samp> | Contains the result of an event listener previously triggered for an event |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">stopImmediatePropagation()</samp> | Immediately prevents the event from rising further during the bubbling phase |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">stopPropagation()</samp> | Prevents the event from rising further during the bubbling phase |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">target</samp> | Contains the element that triggered the event |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">timeStamp</samp> | Contains a timestamp indicating the time when the event was triggered |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">type</samp> | Contains the type of the event |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">which</samp> | In the case of mouse or keyboard events, contains the mouse button or key on the keyboard that was pressed |

**Table 10.24**     Properties and Methods of the Event Object

[Listing 10.24](#10_003.html_l10.24) shows an example of how you can access this information. Most importantly, you can also see here that it’s possible to pass an event a data object that you can then access within the event listener.

```
$('input').on(
  'change,
  {
    value : 4711                       // Data object
  },
  (event) => {
    console.log(event.currentTarget);  // current element
    console.log(event.data);           // data object
    console.log(event.data.value);     // property of the data object
    console.log(event.pageX);          // x position of mouse
    console.log(event.pageY);          // y position of mouse
  }
); 
```

**Listing 10.24**     Accessing the jQuery Event Object

## 10.4    Creating Ajax Requests

Generating Ajax requests is also considerably simplified by jQuery. In this section, we’ll show you how to perform the examples in [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9) for Ajax-based loading of HTML, XML, and JSON data via the appropriate jQuery methods.

### 10.4.1    Creating Ajax Requests

For creating Ajax requests, jQuery provides several methods, listed in [Table 10.25](#10_004.html_t10.25). These are methods that—with the exception of the <samp class="listingcharacter">load()</samp> method—are called not on a selection of elements, as has been the case so far in this chapter, but directly on the <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> object. Therefore, we call these methods global jQuery methods ahead.

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$.ajax()</samp> | Performs an asynchronous HTTP request |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$.get()</samp> | Performs an HTTP request using the HTTP <samp class="listingcharacter">GET</samp> method |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$.getJSON()</samp> | Performs an HTTP <samp class="listingcharacter">GET</samp> request to load JSON data from a server |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$.getScript()</samp> | Performs an HTTP <samp class="listingcharacter">GET</samp> request to load JavaScript data from a server and execute it directly |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">load()</samp> | Performs an HTTP <samp class="listingcharacter">GET</samp> request to load HTML data from a server and embed it directly into the selected elements |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">$.post()</samp> | Performs an HTTP request using the HTTP <samp class="listingcharacter">POST</samp> method |

**Table 10.25**     Main Methods for Working with Ajax

The jQuery global method <samp class="listingcharacter">ajax()</samp> (or <samp class="listingcharacter">$.ajax()</samp>) allows you to create arbitrary Ajax requests. The configuration object expected by this method gives you the most leeway regarding the configuration of a request.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">get()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">post()</samp> methods are used to create <samp class="listingcharacter">GET</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">POST</samp> requests, meaning that you don't have to worry about specific configurations for these request types, such as specifying the HTTP method.

In addition, special methods are available for loading HTML data (<samp class="listingcharacter">load()</samp>), loading JSON data (<samp class="listingcharacter">getJSON()</samp>), and loading JavaScript files (<samp class="listingcharacter">getScript()</samp>).

[Listing 10.25](#10_004.html_l10.25) shows an example of using the <samp class="listingcharacter">ajax()</samp> method, which you already know about in principle from [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9): the goal is to load JSON data from the server and dynamically create a table for this data.

The URL for the request is configured via the <samp class="listingcharacter">url</samp> property of the configuration object, the type expected as a response via the <samp class="listingcharacter">dataType</samp> property (possibilities include, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">json</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">xml</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">html</samp>), and the type of the request via the <samp class="listingcharacter">type</samp> property. Callback functions for the successful execution of a request or also for errors can be defined via the <samp class="listingcharacter">success</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">error</samp> properties. Within the <samp class="listingcharacter">success</samp> callback function, the response of the server is accessed via the <samp class="listingcharacter">data</samp> parameter in the example. Because this is JSON data, it can be processed directly to create the table, as already mentioned.

```
'use strict';
$(document).ready(() => {
  $.ajax({
    url: 'artists.json',
    dataType: 'json',
    type: 'GET',
    success: (data) => {
      const table = initTable();
      const artists = data.artists;
      for (let i = 0; i < artists.length; i++) {
        const artist = artists[i];
        const albums = artist.albums;
        for (let j = 0; j < albums.length; j++) {
          const album = albums[j];
          const row = createRow(
            artist.name,
            album.title,
            album.year
          );
          $(table).find('tbody').append(row);
        }
      }
      $('#artists-container').append(table);
    },
    error: (jqXHR, errorMessage, error) => {
    }
  });
}); 
```

**Listing 10.25**     Generating an Ajax Request

As an alternative to specifying the callback functions via the <samp class="listingcharacter">success</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">error</samp> properties, you also have the option of defining them via the <samp class="listingcharacter">done()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">fail()</samp> methods, which (thanks to jQuery's Fluent API) can be combined directly with calling the <samp class="listingcharacter">ajax()</samp> method (see [Listing 10.26](#10_004.html_l10.26)).

```
'use strict';
$(document).ready(() => {
  $.ajax({
    url: 'artists.json',
    dataType: 'json',
    type: 'GET'
  })
  .done((data) => {
    const table = initTable();
    const artists = data.artists;
    for (let i = 0; i < artists.length; i++) {
      const artist = artists[i];
      const albums = artist.albums;
      for (let j = 0; j < albums.length; j++) {
        const album = albums[j];
        const row = createRow(
          artist.name,
          album.title,
          album.year
        );
        $(table).find('tbody').append(row);
      }
    }
    $('#artists-container').append(table);
  })
  .fail((jqXHR, errorMessage, error) => {
  });
}); 
```

**Listing 10.26**     Generating an Ajax Request via the Fluent API

### 10.4.2    Responding to Events

For responding to events related to working with Ajax requests, jQuery provides the methods shown in [Table 10.26](#10_004.html_t10.26).

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ajaxComplete()</samp> | Specify an event listener that is called when an Ajax request completes |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ajaxError()</samp> | Specify an event listener for errors |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ajaxSend()</samp> | Specify an event listener that is called when an Ajax request is sent |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ajaxStart()</samp> | Specify an event listener that is called when the first Ajax request is started |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ajaxStop()</samp> | Specify an event listener that is called when all Ajax requests have completed |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ajaxSuccess()</samp> | Specify an event listener that is called whenever an Ajax request completes successfully |

**Table 10.26**     Methods for Handling Ajax Events

An example is shown in [Listing 10.27](#10_004.html_l10.27). There are two things to keep in mind here: first, the methods are each called on a selection of elements (or the corresponding jQuery object); second, the event listeners each have a different number of parameters. The event listeners for <samp class="listingcharacter">ajaxStart()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">ajaxStop()</samp> have no parameters at all, the event listeners for <samp class="listingcharacter">ajaxSend()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">ajaxComplete()</samp> each get the event object, plus an object representing the Ajax request and an object with configurations related to the request. The event listeners for the <samp class="listingcharacter">ajaxSuccess()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">ajaxError()</samp> methods also receive the response data and the error object, respectively.

```
$(document)
  .ajaxStart(() => {
    console.log('Request started.');
  })
  .ajaxSend((event, request, settings) => {
    console.log('Request sent.');
  })
  .ajaxSuccess((event, request, settings, data) => {
    console.log('Request completed successfully');
  })
  .ajaxError((event, request, settings, error) => {
    console.log('Error on request: ' + error);
  })
  .ajaxComplete((event, request, settings) => {
    console.log('Request completed.');
  })
  .ajaxStop(() => {
    console.log('All requests completed.');
  }); 
```

**Listing 10.27**     Registering Different Event Listeners for Ajax Events

### 10.4.3    Loading HTML Data via Ajax

To load HTML data via Ajax, you can proceed as in [Listing 10.28](#10_004.html_l10.28) and use the global jQuery <samp class="listingcharacter">get()</samp> method. The important thing here is that you pass the value <samp class="listingcharacter">html</samp> to the <samp class="listingcharacter">dataType</samp> property. You can then use <samp class="listingcharacter">html()</samp> in the corresponding callback function to assign the response data directly to an element as HTML content.

```
'use strict';
$(document).ready(() => {
  const login = $('#login');
  const register = $('#register');
  login.click((e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    loadContent('login');
  });
  register.click((e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    loadContent('register');
  });
});

function loadContent(name) {
  $.get({
    url: name + '.html', 
 dataType: 'html'
  }).done((data) => {
    $('#main-content').html(data);
  });
} 
```

**Listing 10.28**     Loading HTML Data via Ajax

But this process is even easier with the <samp class="listingcharacter">load()</samp> method, as shown in [Listing 10.29](#10_004.html_l10.29). You can call this method directly on a jQuery object (or the selection of elements it represents). As arguments, you pass the URL from which the HTML data should be loaded and optionally a callback function that will be called when the data has been successfully loaded.

```
function loadContent(name) {
  $('#main-content').load(
    name + '.html',
    (
      responseText, 
      textStatus, 
      jqXHRObject
    ) => {
     console.log('HTML loaded');
    }
  );
} 
```

**Listing 10.29**     Alternative Loading of HTML Data via Ajax

###### Sending Additional Data with the Request

You can optionally insert another argument between the URL and the callback function—namely to define the data to be sent to the server with the request (in the form of a string). This is useful, for example, if the server is to generate either this or that response based on the data.

### 10.4.4    Loading XML Data via Ajax

To load XML data, use the <samp class="listingcharacter">get()</samp> method as shown in [Listing 10.30](#10_004.html_l10.30), passing the <samp class="listingcharacter">xml</samp> value for the <samp class="listingcharacter">dataType</samp> property. Within the callback function, the response data is then directly available as XML or as a DOM tree. The best thing about this is that the jQuery <samp class="listingcharacter">$()</samp> method can also use it—for example, to select all <samp class="listingcharacter"><artist></samp> elements using the <samp class="listingcharacter">find()</samp> method as shown in the listing, to iterate over these elements using <samp class="listingcharacter">each()</samp> (another helper method of jQuery, by the way), or to access the text content of the <samp class="listingcharacter"><title></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter"><year></samp> elements using <samp class="listingcharacter">text()</samp>.

```
'use strict';
$(document).ready(() => {
  $.get({
    url: 'artists.xml',
    dataType: 'xml'
  }).done((data) => {
    const table = initTable();
    const artists = $(data).find('artist');
 artists.each((index, artist) => {
      const albums = $(artist).find('album');
 albums.each((index, album) => {
        const row = createRow(
          artist.getAttribute('name'),
          $(album).find('title').text(),
          $(album).find('year').text()
        );
        $(table).find('tbody').append(row);
      });
    });
    $('#artists-container').append(table);
  });
}); 
```

**Listing 10.30**     Loading XML Data via Ajax

### 10.4.5    Loading JSON Data via Ajax

We showed you how to load JSON data using jQuery at the beginning of [Section 10.4.1](#10_004.html_h10.4.1) using the <samp class="listingcharacter">ajax()</samp> method. [Listing 10.31](#10_004.html_l10.31) shows the equivalent example using the <samp class="listingcharacter">get()</samp> method. You specify <samp class="listingcharacter">json</samp> as the value for the <samp class="listingcharacter">dataType</samp> property and can then access the JSON data sent by the server in the callback function as usual.

```
'use strict';
$(document).ready(() => {
  $.get({
    url: 'artists.json',
    dataType: 'json'
  }).done((data) => {
    const table = initTable();
    const artists = data.artists;
    for (let i = 0; i < artists.length; i++) {
      const artist = artists[i];
      const albums = artist.albums;
      for (let j = 0; j < albums.length; j++) {
        const album = albums[j];
        const row = createRow(
          artist.name,
          album.title,
          album.year
        );
        $(table).find('tbody').append(row);
      }
    }
    $('#artists-container').append(table);
  });
}); 
```

**Listing 10.31**     Loading JSON Data via Ajax

Alternatively, jQuery provides the <samp class="listingcharacter">getJSON()</samp> method, which further simplifies requesting JSON data (see [Listing 10.32](#10_004.html_l10.32)). As arguments, you pass this method the URL to be requested and a callback function to access the JSON data sent by the server.

```
'use strict';
$(document).ready(() => {
  $.getJSON(
    'artists.json',
    (
      data, 
      textStatus, 
      jqXHRObject
    ) => {
      // here is the already known content
    }
  );
}); 
```

**Listing 10.32**     Alternative Loading of JSON Data via Ajax

###### Sending Additional Data with the Request

As you saw with the <samp class="listingcharacter">load()</samp> method, you can optionally specify one more argument between the URL and the callback function to define those data that should be sent to the server with the request.

## 10.5    Summary

In this chapter, you learned about the popular jQuery JavaScript library, which simplifies many things, especially with regard to DOM manipulation, event handling, and creating Ajax requests. The following list summarizes the most important aspects:

*   jQuery is a library that mainly hides browser-specific details and provides helper methods for recurring tasks that can be used across browsers.

*   The linchpin for working with jQuery is the <samp class="listingcharacter">jQuery()</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">$()</samp> method.

*   Among other things, you can pass a selector, an existing element, or an HTML string as an argument to this method.

*   As a return value, the method provides a wrapper object (jQuery object) that extends the corresponding elements by additional methods (jQuery methods).

*   Thus, a jQuery object provides various methods for working with the DOM, including the following:

    *   Methods to access the content of elements

    *   Methods to filter selected elements

    *   Methods to access attributes

    *   Methods to access CSS properties

    *   Methods to navigate between elements

    *   Methods to animate elements or their CSS properties

*   For working with events, jQuery provides several methods to register event listeners, including the following:

    *   Methods to register event listeners for general events

    *   Methods to register event listeners for mouse events

    *   Methods to register event listeners for keyboard events

    *   Methods to register event listeners for form events

*   Creating Ajax requests is also made easier by a number of helper methods, including the following:

    *   A method to create arbitrary Ajax requests

    *   A method to create <samp class="listingcharacter">GET</samp> requests

    *   A method to create <samp class="listingcharacter">POST</samp> requests

    *   A method to load HTML content directly into an element via Ajax

    *   A method to load JavaScript files

    *   A method to load JSON files

*   Most helper methods can be used for various purposes; for example, HTML attributes can be both read and written via the <samp class="listingcharacter">attr()</samp> method, CSS properties can be read and written via the <samp class="listingcharacter">css()</samp> method, and event listeners can be registered or removed again via the event methods.

Finally, [Table 10.27](#10_005.html_t10.27) compares how different problems can be handled with jQuery and with pure JavaScript. For more examples, we recommend looking at the [http://youmightnotneedjquery.com](http://youmightnotneedjquery.com) website mentioned earlier. There you can see very nicely how the code of both variants is about equally compact, especially in the DOM manipulation area. When working with events and with Ajax, the code is still a bit more compact with jQuery. In all cases, however, it’s true that jQuery is largely browser-independent, while this doesn’t always apply to the pure JavaScript variants.
